**Chapter Three**

On the explanation of His saying: ﴿the All-Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, and it contains benefits.

**The first benefit:** Al-Rahman is the One who bestows blessings of a kind whose like cannot be conceived as proceeding from the servants. Al-Rahim is the One who bestows blessings of a kind whose like can be conceived as proceeding from the servants. It is reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that he said: "I was a guest of some people, and they set out the meal. A raven descended and snatched a loaf of bread. I followed it in wonder, and it descended into some hills. There I found a man bound, his two hands tied. The raven dropped that loaf upon his face."

It is related from Dhu al-Nun that he said: "I was in the house when a great distress (*walwala*) fell upon my heart, and I reached a state in which I could not control myself. So I left the house and went to the bank of the Nile. There I saw a strong scorpion running, so I followed it. It reached the edge of the Nile, and I saw a frog standing at the edge of the valley. The scorpion leapt onto the frog's back, and the frog began to swim and move away. I boarded a boat and followed it, and the frog reached the other bank of the Nile. The scorpion dismounted from its back and began to run, so I followed it. I saw a young man sleeping under a tree, and I saw a viper heading toward him. When the viper drew near that young man, the scorpion reached the viper, leapt upon it and stung it. The viper also stung the scorpion, and both died together, and the human being was saved from both of them."

It is also related that the chick of the crow, as it emerges from the shell of the egg, comes out without feathers, so that it looks like a piece of red flesh. The crow flees from it and does not take care of raising it. Then gnats gather around it, because it resembles a piece of dead flesh. When the gnats reach it, it seizes those gnats and feeds on them. It continues in this state until it grows strong, its feathers sprout, and its flesh is hidden beneath its feathers. At that point its mother returns to it. For this reason the Arabs' supplications include: "O Provider of the young crow in its nest." Through these examples it becomes clear that God's grace is general, His kindness is all-encompassing, and His mercy is vast.

[p. 190]

Know that events are of two kinds. Some of them are thought to be mercy, though they are not so; rather, in reality they are punishment and vengeance. Others are apparently thought to be punishment and vengeance, though in reality they are grace, kindness and mercy.

As for the first kind: a father who neglects his son, letting him do whatever he wishes, not disciplining him and not compelling him to learn, this appears to be mercy but is in reality vengeance. As for the second kind: like a father who confines his son in the school and compels him to learn. This appears to be vengeance, but in reality it is mercy. Likewise, a person into whose hand gangrene (*al-akila*) has spread, and then that hand is amputated: this appears outwardly to be punishment, but inwardly it is ease and mercy. The fool is deceived by appearances, while the intelligent person looks into the hidden realities.

Once you know this, everything in the world of trial, calamity, pain and hardship, though it appears to be punishment and pain outwardly, is in reality wisdom and mercy. Its verification is what has been said about wisdom: abandoning abundant good for the sake of a little evil is great evil. The purpose of the obligations is the purification of souls from bodily attachments, as the Exalted said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7]. The purpose of creating the Fire is to turn the wicked toward the works of the righteous, and to draw them from the house of flight to the house of abode, as the Exalted said: ﴿So flee to God﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 50].

The closest example for this chapter is the story of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. Musa used to base judgment on the outward appearances of matters, so he disapproved of the scuttling of the ship, the killing of the boy, and the rebuilding of the leaning wall. As for al-Khidr, he based his rulings on realities and secrets, so he said: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who work on the sea, and I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seizes every ship by force﴾; ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief﴾; ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾; ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 79–82].

Through this story it becomes clear that the wise and discerning person is the one who bases his affair on realities rather than on appearances. So when you see what your nature dislikes and what your intellect recoils from, know that beneath it are hidden secrets and far-reaching wisdoms, and that His wisdom and His mercy necessitated it. At that point there appears to you a trace from the seas of the secrets of His words: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

The second benefit: *al-Rahman* is a name specific to God, while *al-Rahim* applies to Him and to others.

If it is said: On this basis, *al-Rahman* is greater, so why did He mention the lesser after mentioning the greater?

The answer: because the great and mighty is not asked for a trivial, small matter. It is related that one of the people went to one of the notables and said: "I have come to you about a minor matter." He said: "Ask for a small matter from a small man." As if the Exalted were saying: If you had confined yourself to mentioning the Most Merciful, you would have been shy before Me, and it would have been difficult for you to ask for small matters. But since you know Me as the Most Merciful, ask Me for great matters. I am also *al-Rahim*; so ask Me for the strap of your sandal and the salt of your cooking pot, just as "the Exalted said to Musa: 'O Musa, ask Me about the salt of your cooking pot and the fodder of your goat.'"

The third benefit: He described Himself as *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim*. Then He gave Maryam, peace be upon her, one single mercy when He said: ﴿And a mercy from Us, and it was a matter decreed﴾ [Maryam: 21]. That mercy became the cause of her deliverance from the reproach of the disbelieving sinners. Then, every day we describe Him thirty-four times as *Rahman* and *Rahim*, because the prayers are seventeen rak'ahs, and the phrase ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ is recited in each rak'ah twice: once in "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," and once in His words: ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. So if the mention of mercy once became a cause for Maryam's deliverance from what is disliked, should not the mention of mercy these many times throughout a lifetime be a cause for the salvation of the Muslims from the Fire, from shame and from ruin?

The fourth benefit: He, exalted is He, is *Rahman* because He creates what the servant cannot create, and *Rahim* because He does what the servant cannot do of its kind. As if the Exalted were saying: I am *Rahman* because you hand over to Me a foul drop, and I hand it back to you in a beautiful form, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. And I am *Rahim* because you hand over to Me deficient obedience, and I hand over to you a pure paradise.

The fifth benefit: "It is related that a youth whose death was near had his tongue seized from pronouncing the testimony that there is no god but God. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of this. He stood and entered upon him, and began to present the testimony to him while he was writhing and convulsing, and his tongue did not work. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Did he not pray? Did he not fast? Did he not give zakat?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Has he disobeyed his parents?' They said: 'Yes.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring his mother.' She came, an old woman who was blind in one eye. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Why do you not pardon him?' She said: 'I will not pardon him, for he struck me and blinded my eye.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring the firewood and fire.' She said: 'What will you do with fire?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I will burn him with fire before your eyes as recompense for what he did to you.' She said: 'I have pardoned, I have pardoned! Did I carry him for nine months for the Fire? Did I nurse him for two years for the Fire? Then where is the mercy of the mother?' At that moment his tongue was released, and he uttered: 'I testify that there is no god but God.'" The point is that she was merciful, but she was not *Rahman*; because of that small measure of mercy, she did not permit burning with fire. So the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, who is not harmed by the offences of His servants, and who cares for His worshippers, how could He permit burning the believer who persisted in the testimony that there is no god but God for seventy years with fire?

The sixth benefit: It is well known that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, had his incisor broken, he said: "O God, guide my people, for they do not know." It is manifest that on the Day of Resurrection he will say: "My community, my community." This is a great generosity from him in this world and in the Hereafter, and this generosity and kindness arose in him only because he is a mercy, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. If the effect of one single mercy is this much, how then is the generosity of One who is *Rahman* and *Rahim*? Also it is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "O God, make the reckoning of my community through my hands." Then he refrained from praying over a deceased person because he had a debt of two dirhams, and he removed Aisha from the house because of the slander. So it is as if the Exalted said to him: You have one mercy, which is His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. A single mercy is not sufficient for the reform of creatures. So leave Me with My servants, and leave Me with your community, for I am the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. My mercy has no end, while their disobedience is finite, and the finite in comparison with the infinite becomes annihilated. Therefore, the disobediences of all creation vanish in the seas of My mercy, because I am the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The seventh benefit: The Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and the human creation of acts) said: How can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who created creatures for the Fire and for eternal punishment? And how can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who creates disbelief in the disbeliever and then punishes him for it? And how can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who commanded faith and then turned away and withheld it from him? The Jabriyya (those who affirm that human beings have no real power over their acts) said: The greatest kind of blessing and mercy is faith. So if faith were not from God, but from the servant, the name *al-Rahman al-Rahim* would be more fitting for the servant than for God. And God knows best.

BOOK FIVE

On the Commentary of Surah al-Fatiha, and it contains chapters.

CHAPTER ONE

On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾, and it contains several aspects.

The first: Here there are three terms: al-hamd (praise/commendation), al-madh (laudation), and al-shukr (thanks). We say: the difference between al-hamd and al-madh is in several respects.

The first: that al-madh may be bestowed upon the living and the non-living. Do you not see that whoever sees a pearl of the utmost beauty or a ruby of the utmost beauty may praise it, whereas it is impossible for him to commend it (ḥamd)? Thus it is established that al-madh is more general than al-ḥamd.

The second aspect of the difference: al-madh may occur before a benefaction and may occur after it, whereas al-ḥamd does not occur except after a benefaction.

The third aspect of the difference: al-madh may be prohibited. He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Throw dust in the faces of those who praise (excessively)." Whereas al-ḥamd is commanded absolutely. He ﷺ said:
صفحة ١٧٩
"Whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah."

The fourth: al-madh is an expression of a statement indicating that the subject is distinguished by a type of virtue, whereas al-ḥamd is a statement indicating that the subject is distinguished by a specific virtue, namely the virtue of bestowing favour and benefaction. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that al-madh is more general than al-ḥamd.

As for the difference between al-ḥamd and al-shukr: al-ḥamd encompasses that benefaction reaching you or reaching someone other than you, whereas al-shukr is specific to the benefaction reaching you.

Having understood this, we say: We have mentioned that al-madh is attributed to the living and the non-living, and to the one who acts by choice and to other than him. So if one said "al-madh lillah" (laudation is for Allah), this would not indicate that He, Exalted, is a chooser-agent. But since he said "al-ḥamd lillah," it indicates that He is a chooser. Thus His words "al-ḥamd lillah" indicate that the speaker affirms that the Lord of the worlds is not an necessitating cause by essence, as the philosophers say, but is a free chooser. Furthermore, His words "al-ḥamd lillah" are preferable to "al-shukr lillah," because "al-ḥamd lillah" is praise of Allah on account of every benefaction that proceeds from Him and reaches others, whereas "al-shukr lillah" is praise on account of a benefaction reaching that speaker. There is no doubt that the first is more excellent, for the implication is as if the servant says: Whether You give me or not, Your benefaction reaches all the worlds, and You deserve the great praise. And it has been said: al-ḥamd is for what Allah has repelled of calamity, and al-shukr is for what He has given of blessings.

If it is said: Blessing in giving is greater than blessing in repelling calamity, so why did He leave the greater and mention the lesser? We say there are several answers:
The first: It is as if he says: I am thankful for the lesser of the two blessings, so how much more for the greater of them.
The second: Withholding (of harm) is unending, while giving is finite, so beginning with thanks for the repelling of calamity, which has no end, is preferable.
The third: that repelling harm is more important than acquiring benefit; therefore He placed it first.

The second point: He, Exalted, did not say "uḥmidu Allah" (I praise Allah), but said "al-ḥamd lillah," and this phrasing is preferable, for several reasons:
One of them: if he had said "uḥmidu Allah," this would indicate that the speaker is capable of praising Him. But since He said "al-ḥamd lillah," it indicates that He was worthy of praise before the praise of the praisers and before the thanks of the thankers. So whether these people praise or do not praise, whether they thank or do not thank, He, Exalted, is praised from eternity to eternity by His eternal praise and His eternal speech.
The second: that our saying "al-ḥamd lillah" means that praise and commendation are a right of Allah and His possession, for He, Exalted, is the one deserving of praise on account of the abundance of His bounties and the varieties of His favours upon the servants. So our saying "al-ḥamd lillah" means that praise belongs to Allah as a right which He deserves in Himself. Had he said "uḥmidu Allah," it would not indicate that He deserves praise in Himself. It is known that a word indicating that He deserves praise is preferable to a word indicating that one particular person praised Him.
The third: that had he said "uḥmidu Allah," he would have praised, but not with praise fitting to Him. But when he says "al-ḥamd lillah," it is as if he says: Who am I that I should praise Him? Yet He is praised by all the praise of the praisers. An example: if you were asked, "Does so-and-so have a favour upon you?" If you say, "Yes," you have praised him, but with weak praise. But if you answer, "Rather, his favours are upon all creatures," you have praised him with the most complete praise.
The fourth: that al-ḥamd is an expression for a quality of the heart, namely the belief that the one praised is bountiful, benevolent, and deserving of veneration and reverence. When a person utters "uḥmidu Allah" while his heart is heedless of the meaning of the veneration befitting the majesty of Allah, he is a liar, for he informs about himself that he is a praiser when he is not so. But when he says "al-ḥamd lillah," whether he is heedless or mindful of the meaning of veneration, he is truthful, for its meaning is that praise is a right of Allah and His possession, and this meaning is present whether the servant is occupied with the meaning of veneration and reverence or not. Thus it is established that His words "al-ḥamd lillah"
صفحة ١٨٠
are preferable to "uḥmidu Allah." Its parallel is our saying "lā ilāha illā Allah," which is not open to falsehood, unlike our saying "ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allah," for one may be lying in his saying "ashhadu." That is why Allah, Exalted, said concerning the refutation of the hypocrites: ﴿Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are liars﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. And for this secret, in the adhan one is commanded to say "ashhadu," and then the conclusion falls upon "lā ilāha illā Allah."

The third point: the lam in His words "al-ḥamd lillah" may carry several meanings:
One of them: appropriate specification, as in your saying: "al-jull lil-faras" (the saddle-cloth is for the horse).
The second: ownership, as in your saying: "al-dār li-Zayd" (the house is Zayd's).
The third: power and dominion, as in your saying: "al-balad lil-sultān" (the land belongs to the sultan).
The lam in your saying "al-ḥamd lillah" may carry these three meanings. If you take it as appropriate specification, it is known that praise befits none but Him, by reason of His utmost majesty and abundance of grace and benevolence. If you take it as ownership, it is known that He, Exalted, owns all things, so He must own, from among them, that they are occupied with praising Him. If you take it as dominion and power, then the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is so; for He is necessary in Himself, and all else is contingent in itself, and the necessary in itself has dominion over the contingent in itself. So "al-ḥamd lillah" means that praise befits none but Him, and means that praise is His possession and He possesses it, and means that He is the one who dominates all and is exalted above all.

The fourth point: His words "al-ḥamd lillah" are eight letters, and the gates of Paradise are eight. Whoever says these eight, from the purity of his heart, deserves the eight gates of Paradise.

The fifth point: al-ḥamd is a singular word to which the definite article has been prefixed, and concerning it there are two opinions:
The first: if it is preceded by a known antecedent, it refers to that; otherwise it is taken to be generic (istighrāq), to safeguard speech from vagueness.
The second opinion: it does not indicate totality, but indicates only the quiddity and reality. Having understood these, we say: His words "al-ḥamd lillah," if we adopt the first opinion, indicate that everything that is praise and commendation belongs to Allah, is His right and His possession; and in that case it follows that what is other than Allah does not deserve praise and commendation at all. If we adopt the second opinion, its meaning is that the quiddity of praise is a right of Allah, Exalted, and His possession, and that negates that any individual instance of this quiddity belongs to other than Allah. Thus it is established on both opinions that His words "al-ḥamd lillah" negate the occurrence of praise to other than Allah.

If it is said: Does not the benefactor deserve praise from the one benefited, and the teacher deserve praise from the student, and the just ruler deserve praise from the subjects? And He, upon him be peace, said: "Whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah."

We say: every one who bestows a favour upon another, the true benefactor is Allah, Exalted; for had Allah not created that motive in the heart of that benefactor, he would not have undertaken that favour; and had Allah not created that blessing and empowered that benefactor over it, and enabled the one benefited to benefit from it, the benefit from that blessing would not have occurred. Thus it is established that the true benefactor is Allah.

* * *

The sixth point: just as His words "al-ḥamd lillah" indicate that no one is praiseworthy except Allah, so too reason indicates this, and its explanation is in several respects:
The first: that if Allah did not create the motive of bestowing favour in the heart of the benefactor, he would not bestow; so the true benefactor is Allah who created that motive.
The second: that everyone who bestows a favour upon another seeks in return for that favour a recompense: either reward, or praise, or the discharge of a right, or the freeing of himself from the trait of miserliness. And one who seeks a recompense is not a benefactor, and so does not truly deserve praise. As for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, He is perfect in His essence, and one perfect in His essence does not seek perfection, for obtaining what is already obtained is impossible. So His gifts are pure generosity and pure benevolence, and therefore He is indeed deserving of praise. Thus it is established
صفحة ١٨١
that none deserves praise except Allah, Exalted.

The third: that every blessing is among the possible existents, and every possible existent came into being by the bringing-into-being of the Truth, either directly or through an intermediary. It follows that every blessing is from Allah, Exalted. This is confirmed by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 53]. And praise has no meaning except commendation for a benefaction; so since there is no benefaction except from Allah, Exalted, it is necessary to be certain that no one deserves praise except Allah, Exalted.

The fourth: a blessing is not complete except when three matters are combined:
One of them: that it be a benefit, and benefiting from a thing is conditional upon its being living and perceiving, and its being living and perceiving is not attained except by the bringing-into-being of Allah, Exalted.
The second: that a benefit is not a complete blessing unless it is free from admixtures of harm and distress, and the freeing of benefits from admixtures of harm is not attained except from Allah, Exalted.
The third: that a benefit is not a complete blessing unless it is safe from fear of cessation, and this matter is not attained except from Allah, Exalted. When this is established, complete blessing is not attained except from Allah, Exalted, so it is necessary that no one deserves complete praise except Allah, Exalted. Thus by these proofs the soundness of His words, Exalted is He, "al-ḥamd lillah" is established.

The seventh point: You have known that praise (ḥamd) is an expression for commending another on account of his being a benefactor and bountiful. And as long as a person does not perceive the arrival of the blessing to him, it is impossible to charge him with praise and thanks. Having understood this, we say: It is necessary that a human being be incapable of praising Allah and thanking Him, and the following considerations show this:
The first: that Allah's blessings upon man are numerous, and the human intellect cannot comprehend them, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And if you should count the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. And if a human being is unable to comprehend them, he is unable to have the power to offer the praise, thanks, and commendation befitting them.

[p. 182]

Second: a person can only give thanks and praise to God if God enables him to do so, if God creates in his heart the motive to perform that praise and gratitude, and if the obstacles and barriers are removed from him. All of this is a bounty from God the Exalted. Accordingly, a person cannot give thanks to God the Exalted except through great blessings from God upon him, and those blessings also require gratitude. On this reasoning, the servant cannot offer thanks and praise except after offering them an endless number of times, and that is impossible. Whatever depends on the impossible is itself impossible. So a person is prevented from offering praise and thanks to God as is fitting for Him.

Third: the meaning of praise and gratitude is not merely a speaker's words with his tongue, "Praise be to God." Rather, their meaning is the recipient of the blessing knowing that the Benefactor is described by the attributes of perfection and majesty. Whatever attributes of perfection and majesty occur to the human mind, the perfection and majesty of God are higher and greater than that which is imagined and conceived. Given this, it is impossible for a person to offer praise, thanks, and commendation to God as He deserves.

Fourth: occupying oneself with praise and gratitude means that the recipient of a blessing responds to the bounty from the Benefactor with thanks and praise from himself. This is remote for several reasons:

The first: God's blessings are numerous and without limit, so responding to them with this single belief and this single word is extremely remote.

The second: whoever believes that his praise and gratitude equal God's blessings has committed shirk (associating partners with God). This is the meaning of the saying of al-Wasiti: "Gratitude is shirk."

The third: a person needs God's bounty in his essence, his attributes, and his states, whereas God is independent of the gratitude of the grateful and the praise of the praisers. So how can God's blessings be matched with this gratitude and this praise? Through these points it is established that the servant is incapable of offering praise and thanks to God. For this subtle reason, God did not say "Praise God," but said "Praise belongs to God," because if He had said "Praise God," He would have burdened them with what they have no ability to bear. When He said "Praise belongs to God," the meaning is that the full extent of praise is His right and His possession, whether or not creation is able to offer it.

It is reported that Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, how can I thank You, when my thanks to You is not complete except by Your bounty upon me, which is that You enable me to give that thanks?" He said: "O Dawud, when you know your incapacity to thank Me, you have indeed thanked Me according to your power and ability."

Eighth benefit: From the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, that he said: "When God bestows a blessing upon His servant, and the servant says, 'Praise be to God,' God the Exalted says: Look at My servant. I gave him what has no measure, and he gave Me what has no worth." Its explanation is that when God bestows a blessing upon a servant, that blessing is one of the customary things, such as when he was hungry and He fed him, or thirsty and He quenched him, or naked and He clothed him. But when the servant says, "Praise belongs to God," its meaning is that every praise offered by any of the praisers belongs to God, and every praise that no one has offered but which the intellect deems possible to come into existence belongs to God. This includes all the praises recited by the angels of the Throne and the Footstool, and the inhabitants of the layers of the heavens; all the praises recited by all the prophets from Adam to Muhammad, may God's blessings be upon them; all the praises recited by all the saints and scholars; and all creation, and all the praises they will recite until the time of their saying: "Their call therein is: Glory be to You, O God, and their greeting therein is peace, and the last of their call is: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" (Yunus 10:10). Then all these praises are finite. But the praises without end are those they will offer forever and ever. All these unending categories are included under the servant's saying: "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds." For this reason God the Exalted said: "Look at My servant. I have given him one blessing that has no measure, and he has given Me gratitude that has no limit and no end."

I say: here is another subtle point. God's blessings upon the servant in this world are finite, while the servant's saying "Praise belongs to God" is unending praise. It is known that when the finite is subtracted from the infinite, what remains is infinite. So it is as if God the Exalted says: "My servant, when you say 'Praise belongs to God' in return for that blessing, what remains for you from that word is endless acts of obedience, so they must be matched with an endless blessing." For this reason, the servant deserves everlasting reward and eternal good. Thus it is established that the servant's saying "to God" brings forth happinesses without end and goods without limit.

* * *

Ninth benefit: There is no doubt that existence is better than non-existence. The proof is that every living being dislikes its own non-existence, and were existence not better than non-existence, it would not be so. Given this, we say: the existence of everything other than God the Exalted came into being through God's creation, His generosity, and His grace. It has been established that existence is a blessing. So it is established that there is nothing existing in the world of spirits and bodies, the higher and the lower realms, except that God has upon it a blessing, mercy, and kindness. Blessing, mercy, and kindness necessitate praise and gratitude. So when the servant says "Praise belongs to God," he does not mean only "Praise belongs to God for the blessings that reach me," but rather "Praise belongs to God for the blessings that proceed from Him." We have shown that His bounty reaches everything other than Him. So when the servant says "Praise belongs to God," its meaning is: praise belongs to God for His bounty upon every creature He created, and upon every thing He brought into being of light and darkness, stillness and motion, throne and footstool, jinn and human, essence and attribute, body and accident, until the end of endless time and the ages of ages. And I bear witness that all of this is entirely Your right and Your possession, and no one has any partnership or contention with You in it.

Tenth benefit: Someone may say: glorification (tasbih) precedes praise (tahmid), because one says "Glory be to God" and then "Praise belongs to God." So what is the reason for beginning here with praise? The answer is that praise indicates glorification by way of implication, for glorification indicates that He is free in His essence and attributes from deficiencies and defects, while praise, given the presence of that attribute, indicates that He is a benefactor to creation, bestowing blessings upon them and being merciful to them. Thus glorification points to God being perfect, while praise indicates that God is beyond perfection. For this reason, beginning with praise is preferable. This point is derived from the philosophical principles (al-qawanin al-hikmiyya). As for the point suited to the principles of jurisprudence (al-qawanin al-usuliyya), it is that God does not benefit His servants unless He has knowledge of all knowable things, so that He knows the kinds of their needs; unless He has power over all possible things, so that He can provide what they need; and unless He is independent of all needs. For if He were not, His occupation with meeting His own need would prevent Him from meeting the need of His servant. It is thus established that His being a benefactor is complete only after His being exempt from deficiencies and defects. Therefore, beginning with His saying "Praise belongs to God" is preferable to beginning with "Glory be to God."

Eleventh benefit: "Praise belongs to God" has a connection with the past and a connection with the future. Its connection with the past is that it is an expression of gratitude for blessings already bestowed. Its connection with the future is that it necessitates the renewal of blessings in the time to come, based on God's saying: "If you are grateful, I will surely increase you" (Ibrahim 14:7). Reason also indicates this, for previous blessings necessitate advancing into service and standing in obedience. Then, when one occupies oneself with gratitude, the doors of God's blessings are opened to the intellect and the heart, along with the doors of knowing Him and loving Him, and that is among the greatest blessings. For this reason, praise, through its connection with the past, closes off from you the doors of the fires, and through its connection with the future, opens to you the doors of the Gardens. Its effect on the past closes the veils between the servant and God the Exalted, and its effect on the future opens the doors of knowing God the Exalted. Since the degrees of God are without end, so the servant's ascent in the stairways of knowing God is also without end, and there is no key to them except our saying "Praise belongs to God." For this reason, the chapter of praise was named the Opening (al-Fatiha).

Twelfth benefit: "Praise belongs to God" is a noble and exalted word, but it must be mentioned in its proper place, or the purpose of it will not be achieved. It was said to al-Sari al-Saqati: "How must one perform acts of obedience?" He said: "For thirty years I have been asking God's forgiveness for one time I said: 'Praise belongs to God.'" It was asked: "How so?" He said: "A fire broke out in Baghdad and burned the shops and houses. They told me that my shop had not burned, so I said: 'Praise belongs to God.' Its meaning was that I rejoiced at the survival of my shop while people's shops were burning, and the right of religion and manliness was that I should not rejoice at that. So I have been asking forgiveness for thirty years for my saying 'Praise belongs to God.'" Through this it is established that although this word is of great worth, it is necessary to observe its proper place. Moreover, God's blessings upon the servant are many, but according to the first division they are limited to two kinds: the blessings of this world and the blessings of religion. The blessings of religion are superior to the blessings of this world for many reasons. Our saying "Praise belongs to God" is a noble and exalted word, so the intelligent person must honor this word and not mention it in return for the blessings of this world; rather, he must mention it only upon attaining the blessings of religion. Then the blessings of religion are of two kinds: acts of the limbs and acts of the heart, and the second kind is more noble. Then the blessings of this world are of two kinds: sometimes those blessings are considered in terms of being blessings, and sometimes they are considered in terms of being the gift of the Benefactor, and the second kind is more noble. These are stations that must be taken into account, so that the mention of our saying "Praise belongs to God" accords with its place and is fitting for its occasion.

Thirteenth benefit: The first word our father Adam spoke was his saying "Praise belongs to God," and the last word the people of Paradise will speak is our saying "Praise belongs to God." As for the first, when the soul reached his navel, he sneezed and said: "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds." As for the second, it is God's saying: "And the last of their call is: Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" (Yunus 10:10). So the opening of the world is founded on praise, and its conclusion is founded on praise. Strive so that the first and last of your deeds are joined with this word, for a human being is a small world, and his states should accord with the states of the great world.

Fourteenth benefit: Some people have said that the implied sense of the sentence is: "Say: Praise belongs to God." In my view this is weak, because implication is resorted to in order for the sentence to be sound, and this implication leads to the corruption of the sentence. What indicates this are the following points:

The first: His saying "Praise belongs to God" is a statement that praise is His right and His possession, and this is a complete sentence in itself, so there is no need for implication.

The second: His saying "Praise belongs to God" indicates that He, the Exalted, deserves praise by virtue of His essence and by virtue of His acts, whether or not they praise Him, because what is so by its own essence is higher and more majestic than what is so by another.

The third point: They mention a question about legal cases, namely that a father should not say to his son, "Do such-and-such," because he may not obey his command and so sin. Rather, he says, "Such-and-such must be done." Then, if the son is generous, he responds and obeys him, and if he is disobedient, he does not reply to him with rejection, so his sin is lesser. Likewise here, God Most High said: "Praise be to God," so whoever is obedient is praised, and whoever is disobedient, his sin is lesser.

* * *

The fifteenth benefit: The Jabriyya (determinists) and the Qadariyya (proponents of human free will) have held onto His saying "Praise be to God." As for the Jabriyya, they have relied on it in several ways:

The first: Whoever's act is more noble and perfect, and whose bestowed blessing is higher and more excellent, deserves more praise. Without doubt, the most noble of created things is faith (iman). So if faith were an act of the servant, the servant's deserving of praise would be more fitting and more exalted than God's deserving of it. Since that is not the case, we know that faith comes about by God's creation, not by the servant's creation.

The second: The community (ummah) has unanimously agreed on their saying, "Praise be to God for the blessing of faith." If faith were an act of the servant and not an act of God, their saying "Praise be to God for the blessing of faith" would be false, for praising the agent for what is not his act is false and ugly, according to His saying: ﴿And they love to be praised for what they did not do﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188].

The third: We have shown that His saying "Praise be to God" indicates, in its outward meaning, that all praise belongs to God, and that there is no praise at all for anyone other than God. All praise would belong to God only if all blessings were from God, and faith is the best of blessings, so it must be that faith is from God.

The fourth: His saying "Praise be to God" is a praise of Himself by Himself, and self-praise is considered reprehensible among created beings. So when He began His Book with praise of Himself, this indicates that His state is different from the state of creatures, and that what is ugly for creatures is fine for God. This indicates that He, the Exalted, is far too holy for His acts to be measured by the acts of creatures. Things may be ugly for servants while those same things are not ugly for God Most High. This completely demolishes the principles of the Mu'tazila.

The fifth: According to the Mu'tazila, God's acts must be good, and must have an additional attribute beyond goodness, otherwise they would be pointless, and that is impossible for Him. The additional attribute beyond goodness is either obligatory or a matter of grace (tafaddul). As for the obligatory, it is like conveying reward and compensation to the accountable (mukallafin). As for what is a matter of grace, it is like His giving more than what is obligatory as a kindness. We say: this undermines His being deserving of praise and invalidates our statement "Praise be to God." The argument goes: As for fulfilling obligations, it does not establish deserving of praise. Do you not see that whoever has a debt of one dinar owed to him by another, and is paid it, does not deserve praise? So if some act were obligatory upon God, that act would only free Him from blame and would not make Him deserving of praise. As for an act of grace, according to the opponent, He gains an increase of praise through it, since if that act had not come from Him, that praise would not have been obtained for Him. And if that is the case, then He would be deficient in Himself and completed by another, and that prevents Him from being deserving of praise
(page 185)
and commendation.

The sixth: His saying "Praise be to God" indicates that He, the Exalted, is praiseworthy. We say: His deserving of praise and commendation is either a matter established for Him by His essence or not established by His essence. If the first, then none of the acts could make Him deserving of praise, because what is established by essence cannot be established by another; and likewise none of the acts could make Him deserving of blame, because what is established by essence cannot be removed by the cause of another. If that is so, then it is not established for God, the Exalted, that anything is obligatory upon Him, and so it is not obligatory for the servants to have any compensation or reward from Him. That demolishes the principles of the Mu'tazila. As for the second division, which is that God's deserving of praise is not established for Him by essence, we say: then it follows that He is deficient in Himself and completed by another, and that is impossible for God. As for the Mu'tazila, they said: His saying "Praise be to God" is only complete according to our doctrine, because the one truly deserving of praise without qualification is the one in whose acts there is no ugliness, in whose decrees there is no injustice, and in whose judgments there is no wrongdoing; and according to us, God is like that, so He deserves the greatest praises and commendations. As for the doctrine of the Jabriyya, there is no ugliness except that it is His act, no injustice except that it is His judgment, and no pointlessness except that it is His making. For He creates disbelief in the disbeliever and then punishes him for it, and He causes pain to animals without compensating them. How, then, can it be conceived under this assumption that He deserves praise? Furthermore, that praise which God deserves by virtue of His divinity is either deserved from the servant or from Himself. If the first, then the servant must be able to act, and that refutes the doctrine of compulsion (jabr). If the second, its meaning would be that God is obligated to praise Himself, and that is false. They said: Thus it is established that the statement "Praise be to God" is only valid according to our doctrine.

The sixteenth benefit: They differed over whether the obligation of gratitude (shukr) is established by reason ('aql) or by revelation (sam'). Among people, some said that it is established by revelation, because of His saying: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra: 15], and His saying: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers﴾ [An-Nisa: 165]. Others said that it is established before the coming of the Law and after its coming, absolutely. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Praise be to God﴾, and its explanation is in several ways:

The first: His saying "Praise be to God" indicates that this praise is His right and His possession absolutely, and that indicates the establishment of this entitlement before the coming of the Law.

The second: He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, and it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that linking a legal ruling to a fitting attribute indicates that the ruling is caused by that attribute. Here, He established praise for Himself, and described Himself as being Lord of the worlds, Most Gracious, Most Merciful towards them, Master of the outcome of their affair on the Day of Resurrection. This indicates that the entitlement to praise arises only because He, the Exalted, is the Cherisher of them, Most Gracious and Most Merciful towards them. If that is so, it is established that the entitlement to praise belongs to God, the Exalted, at all times, whether before or after the coming of the Prophet.

The seventeenth benefit: We must investigate the reality and essence of praise (hamd). We say: God's praise is not an expression of our saying "Praise be to God," because our saying "Praise be to God" is a report about the occurrence of praise, and reporting about a thing is different from the thing reported. Therefore God's praise must be different from our saying "Praise be to God." We say: praising the benefactor (al-mun'im) is an expression of every act that indicates glorification of the benefactor by reason of his being a benefactor. That act is either an act of the heart, or an act of the tongue, or an act of the limbs. As for an act of the heart, it is to believe that He is described by the attributes of perfection and majesty. As for an act of the tongue, it is to utter words indicating that He is described by the attributes of perfection. As for an act of the limbs, it is to perform actions indicating that that benefactor is described by the attributes of perfection and majesty. This is what is meant by praise. Know that the people of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm) have divided at this point
(page 186)
into two groups. The first group: those who said that it is not permissible for God to command His servants to praise Him. They argued for this with several points:

The first: that such praise is either based on a blessing that has reached them or not, and based on it. The first is false, because this would imply that He demanded from them a recompense and reward for His blessing, and that undermines perfection of generosity, for a generous person who bestows does not seek return. As for the second, it is causing hardship to another without prior cause, and that entails injustice.

The second: They said: occupation with this praise is burdensome to the one praising and not beneficial to the one praised, because He is complete in His essence, and what is complete in its essence is impossible to complete by another. Thus it is established that occupation with this praise is pointless and harmful, so it must not be prescribed.

The third: that the meaning of obligation is that if one does not do it, one deserves punishment. So the obligation to praise God means that He said: if you do not occupy yourself with this praise, I will punish you; and this praise has no benefit for God, so its meaning is that this act has no benefit for anyone, and if you abandon it, I will punish you forever and ever; and this is not befitting of the Wise, the Generous Judge. The second group: They said: occupation with praising God is bad manners in several respects:

The first: that it amounts to matching God's favour with that small thanks.

The second: that occupation with gratitude cannot be achieved except with the presence of those blessings in the heart, and the heart's occupation with blessings prevents it from being absorbed in knowledge of the Benefactor.

The third: that praising God at the time of receiving a blessing indicates that he praised Him only for the sake of attaining those blessings, and that indicates that his aim in worship, praise and commendation is attaining those blessings. This person, in reality, his object of worship and purpose is that blessing and the portion of the self, and that is a lowly station. And God knows best.

The second section
On the explanation of His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, and in it are benefits.

The first benefit: Know that the existent is either necessary in its essence (wajib li-dhatihi) or possible in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). As for the necessary in essence, it is God alone, the Exalted. As for the possible in essence, it is everything other than God, the Exalted, and that is the world ('alam). For the theologians (mutakallimun) said: the world is every existent other than God. The reason this category is named "world" is that the existence of everything other than God indicates the existence of God, the Exalted. For this reason every existent other than God is called a world. Having known this, we say: everything other than God, the Exalted, is either a spatially occupying entity (mutahayyiz), or an attribute of a spatially occupying entity, or neither a spatially occupying entity nor an attribute of one. These are three categories:

The first category, the spatially occupying: it is either divisible or not divisible. If divisible, it is body (jism); if not, it is the indivisible atom (jawhar fard). As for body, it is either one of the upper bodies or one of the lower bodies. As for the upper bodies, they are the spheres and the stars. Other things have been established by revelation beyond these two categories, such as the Throne ('arsh), the Footstool (kursi), the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha), the Preserved Tablet (lawh), the Pen (qalam), and Paradise (jannah). As for the lower bodies, they are either simple or compound. As for the simple, they are the four elements:
One of them: the sphere of the earth with what is in it of deserts, mountains and inhabited lands.
The second: the sphere of water, which is the encompassing sea, and these great seas present in this inhabited quarter, and what is in it of great rivers, whose number none knows but God, the Exalted.
The third: the sphere of air.
The fourth: the sphere of fire. As for compound bodies, they are plants, minerals and animals, with their many divisions and varied kinds.

As for the second category, the possible that is an attribute of spatially occupying entities, these are accidents ('arad), and the theologians have mentioned nearly forty genera of accidents.

[Page 187]

As for the third, which is the possible (mumkin) that is neither a body (mutahayyiz) nor an attribute of a body, it is the spirits (al-arwah). They are either lower (suflIyyah) or higher (ulwiyyah). The lower spirits are either good, namely the righteous jinn, or evil and wicked, namely the rebellious devils (marada al-shayatin). The higher spirits are either attached to bodies, namely the celestial spirits (al-arwah al-falakiyyah), or not attached to bodies, namely the pure and holy spirits. This, then, is an indication of the division of the existents of the world. Even if a person wrote a thousand thousand volumes explaining these divisions, he would not reach the least of their levels. However, since it has been established that the Necessarily Existent in Himself (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi) is One, it is established that everything other than Him is possible in itself, and so it is in need, in its existence, of the bringing into being by the Necessarily Existent. It is also established that the possible, during its continuance, does not stand independent of the One who sustains it. Allah the Exalted is the God of the worlds (ilah al-'alamin) insofar as He is the One who brought them out from non-existence into existence, and He is the Lord of the worlds (rabb al-'alamin) insofar as He is the One who sustains them during their continuance and stability. When you know this, a little of the explanation of His saying, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds," will become clear to you. Whoever has the greater comprehension of the states of these three divisions will have the greater understanding of the explanation of His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

**The second benefit:** The one who nurtures (al-murabbi) is of two kinds. The first is one who nurtures something so that the nurturer may profit from it. The second is one who nurtures it so that the one nurtured may profit. The nurturing of all creation is of the first kind, because they nurture others only so that they may profit from them, either through reward or praise. The second kind is the Truth, glory be to Him, as He said: "I created you so that you may profit from Me, not so that I may profit from you." So He, exalted is He, nurtures and bestows goodness, and this is unlike all other nurturers and unlike all other benefactors.

Know that His nurturing, exalted is He, differs from the nurturing of others, and this is explained in several respects:

The first: what we have mentioned, that He, exalted is He, nurtures His servants not for the sake of His own purpose but for their sake, whereas others nurture for the sake of their own purposes and not for the sake of others.

The second: that when another nurtures, the deficiency appears in his treasuries and in his wealth to the extent of that nurturing, whereas He, exalted is He, is exalted above deficiency and harm, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

The third: that when a poor person insists upon another benefactor, that benefactor hates him and withholds and refuses him, whereas the Truth, exalted is He, is not like that. As the Prayer and peace be upon him said: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, loves those who persist in supplication."

The fourth: that another benefactor does not give unless he is asked for the benefaction, whereas the Truth, exalted is He, gives before the request. Consider that He nurtured you while you were an embryo in the womb of your mother, and while you were ignorant and without intellect, unable to ask of Him. He protected you and did good to you, even though you had not asked Him, and you had neither intellect nor guidance.

The fifth: that another benefactor's benefaction ends, either because of poverty, absence, or death, whereas the benefaction of the Truth, exalted is He, never ends at all.

The sixth: that another benefactor's benefaction is restricted to one people and not another, and he cannot generalize it, whereas the nurturing and benefaction of the Truth, exalted is He, has reached everyone, as He said: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, is the Lord of the worlds and a benefactor to all creatures. Therefore He, exalted is He, said concerning Himself: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

**The third benefit:** Whoever is praised, commended, and glorified in this world is so only for one of four reasons:

Either because he is perfect in his essence and attributes, free of all deficiencies and defects, even if no benefaction has come from him to you.

Or because he is good to you and bestows favor upon you.

Or because you hope for the arrival of his benefaction to you in the future.

Or because you are fearful of his subjugation, his power, and the perfection of his might. These states are the grounds that necessitate glorification. It is as if He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is saying: If you are among those who glorify essential perfection, then praise Me, for I am the God of the worlds, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾. If you are among those who glorify benefaction, then I am the Lord of the worlds. If you glorify out of hope for the future, then I am ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. And if you glorify out of fear, then I am ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾.

[Page 188]

**The fourth benefit:** The ways in which Allah nurtures the servant are numerous and countless, and we mention some of them as examples.

**The first example:** When the drop of semen (nutfah) passes from the loins of the father into the womb of the mother, observe how it first becomes a clinging clot ('alaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), and then from it various organs develop, such as bones, cartilage, ligaments, tendons, veins, and arteries. Then some of them become connected to others, and in each of them a particular kind of faculty arises: the faculty of sight in the eye, hearing in the ear, and speech in the tongue. ﴿Glory be to the One who gave hearing through bone, sight through fat, and speech through flesh.﴾ Know that the book of anatomy of the human body is well known, and all of this indicates Allah's nurturing of the servant.

**The second example:** When a single seed falls into the earth, and the moisture of the earth reaches it, it swells, and it splits only from its upper and lower parts, although the swelling occurs from all sides. The upper split produces the part that rises as the tree, and the lower split produces the part that sinks into the earth, which is the roots of the tree. As for the rising part, after it rises it becomes a trunk, and from that trunk many branches separate. Then blossoms first appear on those branches, and then fruits. Those fruits have parts of differing density and fineness: the peels, then the pulp, then the oils. As for the sunken part of the tree, its roots end in tips, and those tips are so fine that they are like condensed waters. Yet despite their extreme fineness, they penetrate the hard, rough earth, and Allah has placed in them attracting powers that draw the fine particles of the clay to themselves. The wisdom in all these arrangements is to provide what the servant needs of nourishment, condiments, fruits, drinks, and medicines, as He said: ﴿Indeed We poured down the water in abundance. Then We split the earth in splitting﴾ [Abasa: 25–26], and so on in the verses.

**The third example:** He placed the celestial spheres and the stars in such a way that they became means for achieving the welfare of the servants. He created the night to be a cause of rest and tranquility, and He created the day to be a cause of livelihood and movement. ﴿It is He who made the sun a shining light and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. ﴿Allah did not create that except in truth﴾. ﴿And it is He who made for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. Recite His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ [al-Naba': 6–7], to the end of the verse. Know that when you reflect on the wonders of the conditions of minerals, plants, and animals, and on the traces of the wisdom of the All-Merciful in the creation of the human being, your clear reason will judge that the causes of Allah's nurturing are numerous, and the signs of His mercy are manifest and evident. At that point there will appear to you a drop from the oceans of the secrets of His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

**The fifth benefit:** He attributed praise to Himself, saying ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, then He attributed Himself to the worlds, the implication being: I love praise. So its attribution to Myself is by way of His being the Owner. Then, when I mentioned Myself, I made Myself known by being the Lord of the worlds. Whoever knows a thing through an attribute tries to mention the best and most perfect of its attributes. This indicates that His being Lord of the worlds is the most perfect of attributes. And the matter is so, because the most perfect of ranks is to be complete, and beyond completeness. Our saying "Allah" indicates that He is Necessarily Existent in Himself, in His essence and by His essence, and this is completeness. His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ means that the existence of everything other than Him flows from His nurturing, His benefaction, and His generosity. This is what is meant by our statement that He is beyond completeness.

**The sixth benefit:** He owns servants other than you, as He said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Yet you have no lord other than Him. Then He nurtures you as though there were no servant of His other than you, while you serve Him as though you had a lord other than Him. How excellent this nurturing is! Does He not protect you during the day from calamities without compensation, and at night from fears without compensation? Know that guards watch over the king every night. But do they guard him against the bite of insects? Do they guard him against misfortunes befalling him? As for the Truth, exalted is He, He guards him from calamities and preserves him from fears, even though He had earlier thrust him at the beginning of the night into various kinds of prohibited acts, divisions of forbidden things, and abominable deeds. How great and how excellent this nurturing is! Is it not part of the nurturing that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The human being is the building of the Lord; cursed is whoever destroys the building of the Lord"? For this meaning He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Who protects you by night and by day from the All-Merciful?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 42]. There is none to do that except the Sovereign, the Mighty, the One, the Subduer, the Turner of hearts and sights, the One who knows the inner thoughts and secrets.

**The seventh benefit:** The Qadariyyah (those who affirm human free will and ability) said: He, exalted is He, is only Lord of the worlds and their nurturer if He is good to them and repels harm from them. But if He creates disbelief in the disbeliever and then punishes him for it, and commands faith and then prevents him from it, He is not a Lord or nurturer; rather He is harmful and injurious. The Jabriyyah (those who deny human agency and affirm absolute divine determinism) said: He would only be Lord and nurturer if blessings came from Him and favors flowed from His mercy. And since faith is the greatest and most sublime of blessings, it must be that its attainment comes from Allah, the Exalted, so that He may be Lord of the worlds, a benefactor to them by creating faith in them.

**The eighth benefit:** Our saying "Allah" is more noble than our saying "Lord (Rabb)," as we have demonstrated with numerous arguments in the explanation of the names of Allah, exalted is He. Moreover, in most cases the supplicant says "O Lord, O Lord." The reason for this is the subtleties and arguments mentioned in the explanation of the names of Allah, exalted is He, so we will not repeat them.

**Chapter Three**

On the explanation of His saying: ﴿the All-Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾, and it contains benefits.

**The first benefit:** Al-Rahman is the One who bestows blessings of a kind whose like cannot be conceived as proceeding from the servants. Al-Rahim is the One who bestows blessings of a kind whose like can be conceived as proceeding from the servants. It is reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that he said: "I was a guest of some people, and they set out the meal. A raven descended and snatched a loaf of bread. I followed it in wonder, and it descended into some hills. There I found a man bound, his two hands tied. The raven dropped that loaf upon his face."

It is related from Dhu al-Nun that he said: "I was in the house when a great distress (*walwala*) fell upon my heart, and I reached a state in which I could not control myself. So I left the house and went to the bank of the Nile. There I saw a strong scorpion running, so I followed it. It reached the edge of the Nile, and I saw a frog standing at the edge of the valley. The scorpion leapt onto the frog's back, and the frog began to swim and move away. I boarded a boat and followed it, and the frog reached the other bank of the Nile. The scorpion dismounted from its back and began to run, so I followed it. I saw a young man sleeping under a tree, and I saw a viper heading toward him. When the viper drew near that young man, the scorpion reached the viper, leapt upon it and stung it. The viper also stung the scorpion, and both died together, and the human being was saved from both of them."

It is also related that the chick of the crow, as it emerges from the shell of the egg, comes out without feathers, so that it looks like a piece of red flesh. The crow flees from it and does not take care of raising it. Then gnats gather around it, because it resembles a piece of dead flesh. When the gnats reach it, it seizes those gnats and feeds on them. It continues in this state until it grows strong, its feathers sprout, and its flesh is hidden beneath its feathers. At that point its mother returns to it. For this reason the Arabs' supplications include: "O Provider of the young crow in its nest." Through these examples it becomes clear that God's grace is general, His kindness is all-encompassing, and His mercy is vast.

[p. 190]

Know that events are of two kinds. Some of them are thought to be mercy, though they are not so; rather, in reality they are punishment and vengeance. Others are apparently thought to be punishment and vengeance, though in reality they are grace, kindness and mercy.

As for the first kind: a father who neglects his son, letting him do whatever he wishes, not disciplining him and not compelling him to learn, this appears to be mercy but is in reality vengeance. As for the second kind: like a father who confines his son in the school and compels him to learn. This appears to be vengeance, but in reality it is mercy. Likewise, a person into whose hand gangrene (*al-akila*) has spread, and then that hand is amputated: this appears outwardly to be punishment, but inwardly it is ease and mercy. The fool is deceived by appearances, while the intelligent person looks into the hidden realities.

Once you know this, everything in the world of trial, calamity, pain and hardship, though it appears to be punishment and pain outwardly, is in reality wisdom and mercy. Its verification is what has been said about wisdom: abandoning abundant good for the sake of a little evil is great evil. The purpose of the obligations is the purification of souls from bodily attachments, as the Exalted said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7]. The purpose of creating the Fire is to turn the wicked toward the works of the righteous, and to draw them from the house of flight to the house of abode, as the Exalted said: ﴿So flee to God﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 50].

The closest example for this chapter is the story of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. Musa used to base judgment on the outward appearances of matters, so he disapproved of the scuttling of the ship, the killing of the boy, and the rebuilding of the leaning wall. As for al-Khidr, he based his rulings on realities and secrets, so he said: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who work on the sea, and I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seizes every ship by force﴾; ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared that he would burden them with tyranny and disbelief﴾; ﴿So we wished that their Lord would replace him with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾; ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 79–82].

Through this story it becomes clear that the wise and discerning person is the one who bases his affair on realities rather than on appearances. So when you see what your nature dislikes and what your intellect recoils from, know that beneath it are hidden secrets and far-reaching wisdoms, and that His wisdom and His mercy necessitated it. At that point there appears to you a trace from the seas of the secrets of His words: ﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

The second benefit: *al-Rahman* is a name specific to God, while *al-Rahim* applies to Him and to others.

If it is said: On this basis, *al-Rahman* is greater, so why did He mention the lesser after mentioning the greater?

The answer: because the great and mighty is not asked for a trivial, small matter. It is related that one of the people went to one of the notables and said: "I have come to you about a minor matter." He said: "Ask for a small matter from a small man." As if the Exalted were saying: If you had confined yourself to mentioning the Most Merciful, you would have been shy before Me, and it would have been difficult for you to ask for small matters. But since you know Me as the Most Merciful, ask Me for great matters. I am also *al-Rahim*; so ask Me for the strap of your sandal and the salt of your cooking pot, just as "the Exalted said to Musa: 'O Musa, ask Me about the salt of your cooking pot and the fodder of your goat.'"

The third benefit: He described Himself as *al-Rahman* and *al-Rahim*. Then He gave Maryam, peace be upon her, one single mercy when He said: ﴿And a mercy from Us, and it was a matter decreed﴾ [Maryam: 21]. That mercy became the cause of her deliverance from the reproach of the disbelieving sinners. Then, every day we describe Him thirty-four times as *Rahman* and *Rahim*, because the prayers are seventeen rak'ahs, and the phrase ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ is recited in each rak'ah twice: once in "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," and once in His words: ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. So if the mention of mercy once became a cause for Maryam's deliverance from what is disliked, should not the mention of mercy these many times throughout a lifetime be a cause for the salvation of the Muslims from the Fire, from shame and from ruin?

The fourth benefit: He, exalted is He, is *Rahman* because He creates what the servant cannot create, and *Rahim* because He does what the servant cannot do of its kind. As if the Exalted were saying: I am *Rahman* because you hand over to Me a foul drop, and I hand it back to you in a beautiful form, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He formed you and perfected your forms﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. And I am *Rahim* because you hand over to Me deficient obedience, and I hand over to you a pure paradise.

The fifth benefit: "It is related that a youth whose death was near had his tongue seized from pronouncing the testimony that there is no god but God. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of this. He stood and entered upon him, and began to present the testimony to him while he was writhing and convulsing, and his tongue did not work. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Did he not pray? Did he not fast? Did he not give zakat?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Has he disobeyed his parents?' They said: 'Yes.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring his mother.' She came, an old woman who was blind in one eye. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Why do you not pardon him?' She said: 'I will not pardon him, for he struck me and blinded my eye.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Bring the firewood and fire.' She said: 'What will you do with fire?' He, peace be upon him, said: 'I will burn him with fire before your eyes as recompense for what he did to you.' She said: 'I have pardoned, I have pardoned! Did I carry him for nine months for the Fire? Did I nurse him for two years for the Fire? Then where is the mercy of the mother?' At that moment his tongue was released, and he uttered: 'I testify that there is no god but God.'" The point is that she was merciful, but she was not *Rahman*; because of that small measure of mercy, she did not permit burning with fire. So the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, who is not harmed by the offences of His servants, and who cares for His worshippers, how could He permit burning the believer who persisted in the testimony that there is no god but God for seventy years with fire?

The sixth benefit: It is well known that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, had his incisor broken, he said: "O God, guide my people, for they do not know." It is manifest that on the Day of Resurrection he will say: "My community, my community." This is a great generosity from him in this world and in the Hereafter, and this generosity and kindness arose in him only because he is a mercy, as the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. If the effect of one single mercy is this much, how then is the generosity of One who is *Rahman* and *Rahim*? Also it is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "O God, make the reckoning of my community through my hands." Then he refrained from praying over a deceased person because he had a debt of two dirhams, and he removed Aisha from the house because of the slander. So it is as if the Exalted said to him: You have one mercy, which is His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya: 107]. A single mercy is not sufficient for the reform of creatures. So leave Me with My servants, and leave Me with your community, for I am the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. My mercy has no end, while their disobedience is finite, and the finite in comparison with the infinite becomes annihilated. Therefore, the disobediences of all creation vanish in the seas of My mercy, because I am the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

The seventh benefit: The Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and the human creation of acts) said: How can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who created creatures for the Fire and for eternal punishment? And how can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who creates disbelief in the disbeliever and then punishes him for it? And how can He be Most Merciful, Especially Merciful, who commanded faith and then turned away and withheld it from him? The Jabriyya (those who affirm that human beings have no real power over their acts) said: The greatest kind of blessing and mercy is faith. So if faith were not from God, but from the servant, the name *al-Rahman al-Rahim* would be more fitting for the servant than for God. And God knows best.
