**Chapter Four: On the Commentary of His Words, "Master of the Day of Judgment" (Maliki yawmi'd-din), and It Contains Several Benefits**

**First benefit:** His words, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, mean the Master of the Day of Resurrection and Recompense. The reasoning is that there must be a distinction between the good-doer and the evildoer, the obedient and the disobedient, the one who conforms and the one who opposes. This distinction does not become manifest except on the Day of Recompense, as the Exalted said: ﴿That He may recompense those who did evil according to what they did, and recompense those who did good with the best [reward]﴾ [al-Najm 53:31]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters in the earth? Or shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad 38:28]. And He said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:15].

Know that whoever empowers the oppressor over the oppressed and then does not avenge him, that is either due to incapacity, or ignorance, or because He is pleased with that injustice. These three attributes are impossible for Allah the Exalted. Therefore it is necessary that He avenge the oppressed against the oppressors. Since this avenging did not occur in the abode of this world, it is necessary that it occur in the abode of the Hereafter after the abode of this world. That is what is meant by His words, ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, and by His words, ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah 99:7] and the rest of the verse.

It is related that a man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and he will look into the state of his own soul, and will see for himself no good deed at all. Then a call will come: "O so-and-so, enter Paradise by your deed." He will say: "My Lord, what have I done?" Allah the Exalted will say: "Did you not, when you were sleeping, turn from side to side on such-and-such a night, and say in the midst of that, 'Allah,' and then sleep overcame you at once, and you forgot that? As for Me, drowsiness does not seize Me, nor sleep, and so I did not forget that."

And also, a man will be brought, and his good deeds and his bad deeds will be weighed. His good deeds will be light, and then a slip [of paper] will be brought to him which will weigh down his scale. Lo, in it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Nothing weighs heavier than the remembrance of Allah.

Know that the obligations are of two kinds: the rights of Allah the Exalted, and the rights of the servants. As for the rights of Allah the Exalted, their basis is leniency, because He the Exalted is free of need from the worlds. As for the rights of the servants, these are the ones that must be guarded against.

It is related that Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, had a claim upon one of the Magians for some money. He went to his house to demand it from him. When he reached the door of his house, a najasa (impurity) fell upon his sandal. He shook his sandal, and the impurity was removed from his sandal and fell upon the wall of the Magian's house. Abu Hanifa was perplexed and said: "If I leave it, that will be a cause of disfigurement to this Magian's wall; and if I scrape it off, the dust will fall from the wall." So he knocked on the door. A maidservant came out, and he said to her: "Tell your master: Abu Hanifa is at the door." The man came out to him, thinking he was demanding the money, and began to make excuses. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Here is something more important." He mentioned the story of the wall and how it could be purified. The Magian said: "I will begin by purifying myself," and he embraced Islam at once. The point in this is that when Abu Hanifa guarded against wronging the Magian in that small measure of wrong, because of his leaving that, the Magian moved from disbelief to faith. So how then will the state of one who guards against wrongdoing be in the sight of Allah the Exalted?

**Second benefit:** The reciters differed regarding this word. Some of them recited ﴿Maliki﴾ (Master), and some of them recited *Maliki* (King of the Day of Judgment, مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ). The argument of those who recited مَالِكِ (*Maliki*) consists of several points:

The first: that it contains an additional letter, so its recitation carries more reward.

The second: that on the Day of Resurrection there will be many kings. The true owner of the Day of Recompense is none other than Allah.

The third: the one who owns (*malik*) may or may not be a king, just as the king may or may not be an owner. Ownership (*milkiyyah*) and mastery (*malikiyyah*) may each be separated from the other. However, mastery is the cause of unrestricted disposal, whereas ownership is not like that. So the Master is preferable.

The fourth: a king is king over subjects (*ra'iyyah*), and a master (*malik*) is master over slaves, and the slave is of lower status than the subject. Therefore, coercion in mastery must be greater than in kingship,

**[p. 193]**

so the Master must be of higher status than the King.

The fifth: subjects are able to remove themselves from being subjects of that king by their own choice, whereas a slave cannot remove himself from being a slave of that master by his own choice. Thus it is established that coercion in mastery is more perfect than in kingship.

The sixth: a king is obligated to care for the condition of the subjects. The Prayer and peace be upon him said: "Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock." But it is not obligatory for the subjects to serve the king. As for the slave, it is obligatory upon him to serve the master, and not to act independently in any matter except with his master's permission. Indeed, his judgeship, leadership of prayer and testimony are not valid from him. When his master intends to travel, he becomes a traveler; and if his master intends to settle, he becomes settled. So we know that submission and subjugation in slavehood are more complete than in being a subject. These are the points indicating that the Master is more perfect than the King.

And the argument of those who said that the King is preferable to the Master consists of several points:

The first: every single person in a city is an owner, but the king is none other than the greatest and highest of people. So the king is more noble than the owner.

The second: they agreed that in the Exalted's words, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ ﴿the King of mankind﴾ [al-Nas 114:1], the word "King" is specified, and if the King were not of higher status than the Master, it would not be specified.

The third: the King is preferable because it is shorter, and it is likely that one will find enough time to complete this word in full, unlike *Malik*, which is longer, so it is possible one may not find enough time to complete this word. This is related from Abu 'Amr. Al-Kisa'i replied by saying: "I begin to mention this word; if I do not reach it, I have nonetheless reached it by resolving upon it." A parallel in the legal rulings: whoever intends to fast the next day before the sunset of the day during the days of Ramadan, it does not suffice him, because during this day he is occupied with fasting this day; when he intends to fast tomorrow, that is prolonging hope. But if he intends after sunset, it does not suffice him, because although that is prolonging hope, he has already exited the fast by the sunset, and he may die that night. So he says: "If I do not reach the day, at least I will be upon the resolve to fast." Likewise here: he begins to mention the word "Malik," and if he completes it, well and good; and if he cannot complete it, he was resolved upon completing it, and that is what is meant.

Then we say: certain rulings branch from His being King, and other rulings branch from His being Master.

As for the rulings branching from His being King, they are several:

The first: that policies are of four kinds: the policy of owners, the policy of kings, the policy of angels, and the policy of the King of Kings. The policy of kings is stronger than the policy of owners, because if a world of owners gathered, they would not be able to oppose a single king. Do you not see that a master does not possess the authority to carry out the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) upon his slave according to Abu Hanifa, whereas they agreed that the king possesses the authority to carry out the prescribed punishments upon people? As for the policy of the angels, it is above the policies of kings, because a world of the greatest kings cannot repel the policy of a single angel. As for the policy of the King of Kings, it is above the policies of the angels. Do you not see His words: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is right﴾ [al-Naba' 78:38], and His words: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255], and He said describing the angels: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:28]. So O kings, do not be deceived by your wealth and kingdom, for you are captives in the grip of the power of the Master of the Day of Judgment. And O subjects, if you fear the policy of the king, do you not fear the policy of the King of Kings, who is the Master of the Day of Judgment?

The second ruling of His being King: that He is a King who is not like other kings, because if they give in charity something, their kingship diminishes and their treasuries decrease. But as for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, His kingship does not diminish by giving and beneficence; rather it increases. Its explanation: when He gives you one child, His command applies only to that one child; but if He gives you ten children, His command and obligation apply to all of them. Thus it is established that the more He gives, the wider His kingdom becomes.

The third ruling of His being King: the perfection of mercy. The evidence for this is verses:

The first of them: what is mentioned in this surah of His being Lord, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The second: His words: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no god, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Hashr 59:22]. Then He said after it: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no god, the King﴾ [al-Hashr 59:23]. Then He mentioned after it His being Holy (*Quddus*), free of injustice and tyranny; then He mentioned after it His being Peace (*Salam*), who has preserved His servants from His injustice and tyranny; then He mentioned after it His being the Giver of Security (*Mu'min*), who grants security to His servants from His tyranny and injustice. Thus it is established that His being King is not complete except with perfect mercy.

The third: His words: ﴿The Kingdom on that Day belongs to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan 25:26]. When He established kingship for Himself, He followed it by describing Himself as the Most Merciful, meaning: if the establishment of kingship for Him on that day indicates perfect dominance, His being the Most Merciful indicates the removal of fear and the attainment of mercy.

The fourth: His words: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ ﴿the King of mankind﴾ [al-Nas 114:1]. He first mentioned His being Lord of mankind, then followed it with His being King of mankind. These verses indicate that kingship is not good nor complete except with beneficence and mercy. So O kings, listen to these verses, show mercy to these poor people, and do not seek a rank in kingship greater than the kingship of Allah the Exalted.

The fourth ruling for the King: it is obligatory upon the subjects to obey him. If they oppose him and do not obey him, chaos and disorder occur in the world, confusion and turmoil arise, and that leads to the ruin of the world and the annihilation of creation. When you have witnessed that opposition to the king who recompenses leads ultimately to the ruin of the world and the annihilation of creation, then consider how the opposition to the King of Kings affects the loss of benefits and the occurrence of harms! The full explanation is that the Exalted has shown that disbelief is a cause of the ruin of the world. He said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent from it, and the earth is split asunder, and the mountains fall in ruins﴾ ﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾ [Maryam 19:90–91]. And He showed that His obedience is a cause of benefits. He said: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer, and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you, and the good end is for righteousness﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:132]. So O subjects, be obedient to your kings; and O kings, be obedient to the King of Kings, so that the benefits of the world may be ordered.

The fifth ruling: when He described Himself as King of the Day of Religion (*yawm al-din*), He manifested to the worlds the perfection of His justice. He said: ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat 41:46]. Then He explained the manner of justice, saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:47]. Thus it became clear by this that His being the true King of the Day of Religion appears only through justice. If the King who recompenses is just, he is a true king; otherwise he is a false king. If he is a just and true king, good and comfort are produced in the world through the blessing of his justice; and if he is an unjust king, goodness is removed from the world.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 1, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

It is related that Anushirwan once went out hunting. He pursued the game far ahead, lost contact with his army, and was overcome by thirst. He came upon an orchard, and when he entered it he saw pomegranate trees. He said to a boy who was present in the orchard: "Give me one pomegranate." The boy gave him a pomegranate, and he split it, took out its seeds, and pressed them, and a large quantity of water came out, which he drank. He was pleased with that pomegranate and resolved to take the orchard from its owner. Then he said to the boy: "Give me another pomegranate." The boy gave him one, and he pressed it, and only a little water came out. He drank it and found it astringent and harmful. He said: "O boy, why has the pomegranate become like this?" The boy said: "Perhaps the king of the land has resolved to commit injustice, and because of the ill omen of his injustice the pomegranate has become like this." Anushirwan repented in his heart of that injustice. He said to the boy: "Give me another pomegranate." The boy gave him one, and he pressed it and found it sweeter than the first pomegranate. He said to the boy: "Why has this condition changed?" The boy said: "Perhaps the king of the land has repented of his injustice." When Anushirwan heard this account from the boy, and it corresponded to the state of his heart, he repented entirely of injustice. Therefore his name remained immortalized in this world through justice. Indeed, some people narrate from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "I was born in the time of the just king."

As for the rulings that follow from His being Master (Malik), there are four:

The first ruling: the reading *Malik* (Master) is more hopeful than the reading *Malik* (King). This is because the most that can be hoped for from a king is justice and fairness, and that a person escape from him scot-free. As for a master, the servant asks from him clothing, food, mercy, and nurture. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: "I am your Master, so upon Me is your sustenance, your reward, and your Paradise."

The second ruling: although a king is richer than a master, the king desires from you, whereas you desire from the master. We have no acts of obedience or good deeds, so He does not wish to ask us on the Day of Resurrection for kinds of good deeds and acts of obedience. Rather, He wishes that we ask Him on the Day of Resurrection for pardon, forgiveness, and the granting of Paradise purely by His bounty. For this reason al-Kisa'i said: recite "﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾" (Master of the Day of Judgment), because this reading is the one that indicates abundant bounty and vast mercy.

The third ruling: when a king reviews his army, he accepts only one who is physically strong and of sound constitution. As for one who is sick, he rejects him and gives him none of what is due. But when a master has a servant, if he falls ill he treats him, if he weakens he helps him, and if he falls into affliction he rescues him. Therefore the recitation with the word *Malik* (Master) is more fitting for sinners and the needy.

The fourth ruling: the king has awe and political authority, while the master has tenderness and mercy. Our need for tenderness and mercy is greater than our need for awe and authority.

The third benefit: sovereignty (al-mulk) is an expression of power. Thus His being Master and King is an expression of power. Here there is a question: He, exalted is He, is either King of existent things or King of non-existent things. The first is false, because bringing existent things into being is impossible, so God has power over existent things only by annihilating them. On this account there is no master except over non-existence. The second is also false, because it entails that His power and sovereignty are over non-existence, and it would follow that God has no mastery or sovereignty over existent things, and this is far-fetched.

The answer is that God, exalted is He, is the Master and King of existent things, in the sense that He is able to transfer them from existence to non-existence, or in the sense that He is able to transfer them from one attribute to another. This power belongs to none but God, exalted is He. So the True King is God, glorified and exalted is He. When you know that He is the True King, we say: He is King of the Day of Religion (Yawm al-Din). This is because the power to revive creation after their death belongs to none but God, and knowledge of those scattered parts of human bodies belongs to none but God. Since gathering, resurrection, raising from the dead, and the Last Day cannot be accomplished except by knowledge connected to all knowables and by power connected to all possibilities, it is established that there is no master of the Day of Religion except God. The full discussion of this section is connected with the question of gathering and resurrection.

If it is said: the master is not a master of a thing unless the owned thing exists, and the Resurrection does not exist at present, so God is not Master of the Day of Religion; rather it must be said "Master of the Day of Religion" (Malik yawm al-din, with the noun in the genitive), as evidence that if one says "I am the killer of Zayd" it is an acknowledgment, but if one says "I am killer Zayd" with tanwin, it is a threat and warning.

We reply: what you have said is correct, except that since the establishment of the Resurrection is a true matter and it is not permissible for wisdom to be neglected, the existence of the Resurrection is treated as a matter that is established and present at this moment. Also, whoever dies, his own resurrection has already occurred, so the Resurrection is present at this moment, and the question is resolved.

The fourth benefit: He, exalted is He, mentioned five of His names in this surah: Allah, al-Rabb (the Lord), al-Rahman (the Most Merciful), al-Rahim (the Especially Merciful), and al-Malik (the Master). The reason is as if He says: "I created you first, so I am God (Ilah). Then I nurtured you with various kinds of blessings, so I am Lord (Rabb). Then you disobeyed, and I concealed it for you, so I am the Most Merciful (Rahman). Then you repented, and I forgave you, so I am the Especially Merciful (Rahim). Then the reward must reach you, so I am Master of the Day of Religion."

If it is said: He mentioned "al-Rahman al-Rahim" in the basmalah once and in the surah a second time, so repetition is present in these two and absent in the three names. What is the wisdom in this?

We reply: the sense is as if it were said: "Remember that I am God and Lord once; and remember that I am Most Merciful and Especially Merciful twice, so that you know that the concern with mercy is greater than with other matters." Then, when He had shown the doubled mercy, it is as if He said: "Do not be deceived by that, for I am Master of the Day of Religion." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: "﴿Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty﴾" (Ghafir 40:3).

The fifth benefit: the Qadariyya (the advocates of free will) said: if the Creator of the acts of servants is God, then it is impossible to affirm reward, punishment, and recompense, because rewarding a person for what he did not do is pointless, and punishing him for what he did not do is injustice. On this supposition, His being Master of the Day of Religion is void. The Jabriyya (the determinists) said: if the acts of servants were not by God's decree and determination, He would not be their Master. Since the Muslims agree that He is the Master of the servants and of their acts, we know that He is their Creator, their Determiner. And God knows best.

**Chapter Five**

On the exegesis of His words ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, and it contains several benefits.

**The first benefit:** *ʿibadah* (worship) is an expression for an act performed for the purpose of venerating another. It is derived from the phrase *ṭarīq muʿabbad*, meaning a path that has been made smooth and trodden. Know that your saying *iyyāka naʿbudu* means: "I do not worship anyone other than You." The following points indicate this restriction:

**The first point:** *ʿibadah* is an expression for the utmost degree of veneration, and it is fitting only for one from whom the utmost bounty has proceeded. The greatest forms of bounty are life, which grants the capacity to benefit, and the creation of that which is benefited from. The first level, which is life granting the capacity to benefit, is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ [Maryam 19:9], and His words: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:28]. The second level, which is the creation of that which is benefited from, is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29]. Since the benefits obtained in this lower world are arranged only through the celestial motions in the manner of the customary course of things, He therefore followed this with His words: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens, and He is Knower of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29]. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that all blessings come into being through the creation of God, exalted is He. Therefore it is obligatory that worship be rendered only to God, exalted is He. For this reason He said *iyyāka naʿbudu*, since His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾ imply restriction.

**The second point, concerning the proofs of this restriction and specification:** God, exalted is He, named Himself here with five names: Allah, al-Rabb (the Lord), al-Raḥmān (the Most Merciful), al-Raḥīm (the Especially Merciful), and Mālik Yawm al-Dīn (Master of the Day of Judgment). The servant has three states: the past, the present and the future. As for the past, he was utterly non-existent, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29]. He was dead, then God gave him life, as He said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:28]. He was ignorant, then God taught him, as He said: ﴿God brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:78]. The servant has only passed from non-existence to existence, from death to life, from incapacity to capacity, and from ignorance to knowledge, because God, exalted is He, is eternal and everlasting. By His eternal power and His eternal knowledge He brought him into being and brought him from non-existence to existence. Therefore He is God (*ilāh*) in this sense.

As for the present state of the servant, his need is intense, because whenever he was non-existent he was in need of the Lord, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Then when he entered into existence, the doors of needs were opened to him and the causes of necessities came into being for him. God, exalted is He, said: "I am God because I brought you out from non-existence into existence." After you became existent, your needs for Me have multiplied, so I am the Lord, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

As for the future state of the servant, it is the state after death, and the attribute related to that state is His saying "﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾". These five attributes of God, exalted is He, have thus become related to these three states of the servant. It becomes clear that all the interests of the servant in the past, the present and the future are not complete or perfected except through God, His grace and His beneficence. Since the matter is so, it is obligatory that the servant not occupy himself with worshipping anything except the worship of God, exalted is He. Therefore the servant says, by way of restriction, ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾.

**The third point, concerning the proof of this restriction:** The decisive proof has indicated that it is necessary that He, exalted is He, be capable, knowing, beneficent, bountiful, generous and forbearing. As for whether anything else is so, it is doubtful. For there is no effect that is ascribed to nature, the sphere, the stars, the intellect or the soul except that its attribution to the power of God, exalted is He, is possible. With this possibility, that ascription becomes doubtful. Thus it is established that knowledge that God, exalted is He, is the one worshipped by creation is a certainty. As for whether anything else is worshipped by creation, that is doubtful. Holding to certainty is preferable to holding to doubt, so it is obligatory to set aside the doubtful and adhere to the known. On this basis there is no one worshipped except God, exalted is He. For this reason He said ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾.

**The fourth point:** Servitude is humiliation and abasement, but the higher and more exalted the master is, the more pleasant and sweet is servitude to him. Since God, exalted is He, is the most noble and most exalted of existents, His servitude is more fitting than the servitude of any other. Also, the power of God, exalted is He, is higher than the power of any other; His knowledge is more complete than the knowledge of any other; His generosity is greater than the generosity of any other. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that His servitude is more fitting than the servitude of any other. For this reason He said ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾.

**The fifth point:** Everything other than the Necessary Existent in Himself is possible in its own essence, and everything that is possible in its own essence is needy and poor. The needy is occupied with the need of his own self, and so he cannot undertake to remove need from others. A thing that does not possess existence in its own essence cannot remove need from another. The One who is self-sufficient in His essence is God, exalted is He. Therefore the remover of needs is God, exalted is He, and the one deserving worship is God, exalted is He. For this reason He said ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾.

**The sixth point:** Deserving worship requires the power of God, exalted is He, to hold up the heaven without a support and the earth without a pillar, to set the sun and the moon in motion, to still the two poles, to bring forth from the clouds at times fire, which is lightning, at times air, which is wind, and at times water, which is rain. As for the earth, at times He brings forth water from stone, which is evident, and at times He brings forth stone from water, which is ice. Then He placed in the earth bodies that remain fixed and do not travel, which are the mountains, and bodies that travel and do not remain, which are the rivers. He caused the earth to swallow Qarun, placing the earth above him. He raised Muhammad, peace be upon him, so that he was [brought] to within two bow-lengths. He made water into fire for the people of Pharaoh, who were drowned and then made to enter fire. He made fire cool and peaceful for Abraham. He lifted Moses above the mountain and said to him, "Take off your sandals," and He raised the mountain over Moses and his people: ﴿And We raised the mountain above them﴾ [al-Nisa 4:154]. He made the dry land drown the world from the oven, according to His saying: ﴿And the oven boiled over﴾ [Hud 11:40]. He made the sea dry for Moses, peace be upon him. So whoever has such power, how can he be equated in worship with others: with inanimate things, plants, animals, humans, the sphere, or a king? The equating of the deficient with the perfect, and of the base with the precious, indicates ignorance and foolishness.

**The second benefit:** His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ indicates that there is no one worshipped except God. When this is so, it is established that there is no god except God. Thus His saying ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾ indicates pure monotheism (*tawḥīd*).

Know that the polytheists (*mushrikūn*) are of several kinds, for everyone who takes a partner with God, that partner is either a body or not a body. As for those who took a corporeal partner, that partner is either of the lower bodies or of the higher bodies. As for those who took partners from the lower bodies, that body is either composite or simple. The composite is either from minerals, plants, animals or humans. As for those who took partners from mineral bodies, they are those who make idols from stones, gold or silver and worship them. As for those who took partners from plant bodies, they are those who took a particular tree as an object of worship for themselves. As for those who took partners from animals, they are those who took the calf as an object of worship for themselves. As for those who took partners from humans, they are those who said: "Uzayr is the son of God," and "the Messiah is the son of God." As for those who took partners from simple bodies, they are those who worship fire, namely the Magians. As for those who took partners from the higher bodies, they are those who worship the sun, the moon and the rest of the stars and ascribe happiness and misfortune to them; they are the Sabians and most astrologers.

As for those who took partners to God other than bodies, they too are of several groups:

The first group: those who said the governor of the world is light and darkness. These are the Manichaeans and the Dualists.

The second group: those who said the angels are expressions of the celestial spirits. For each region there is a specific celestial spirit that governs it, and for each kind of this world there is a celestial spirit that governs it. They take images and statues for those spirits and worship them. These are the worshippers of angels.

The third group: those who said the world has two gods: one good and the other evil. They said: the governor of this world is God, exalted is He, and Iblis, and they are two brothers. Whatever good is in the world is from God, and whatever evil is in it is from Iblis.

Having known these details, we say: everyone who takes a partner for God must necessarily be preceded in worshipping that partner in some respect, either seeking its benefit or fleeing from its harm. As for those who persisted in monotheism, rejected the doctrine of partners and rivals, and worshipped none but God, and turned to none other than God, their hope was in God, their fear was of God, their desire was for God, and their awe was of God. Therefore they worshipped none but God and sought help from none but God. For this reason they said ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, so His saying ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾ stands in place of His saying "there is no god but God."

Know that the well-known dhikr is that you say: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except by God, the Most High, the Mighty." We have shown that our saying "Praise be to God" includes within it the meaning of our saying "Glory be to God," because His saying "Glory be to God" indicates that He is perfect and complete in His essence, and His saying "Praise be to God" indicates that He is the one who completes and perfects others. Something cannot complete and perfect others unless it was before that already perfect and complete in its essence. Thus it is established that our saying "Praise be to God" includes within it the meaning of our saying

[Page 199]

"Glory be to God." When He said "Praise be to God," affirming all kinds of praise, He mentioned that which serves as the reason for affirming all kinds of praise to God, so He described Himself with the five attributes, which are those by which the interests of the servant are perfected in the three times, as we have explained. When this was made clear, the correctness of our saying "Glory be to God and praise be to God" was established. Then He mentioned after it His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾, and we have shown that it stands in place of "there is no god but God." Then He mentioned His saying ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾, and its meaning is that God, exalted is He, is too high, too majestic and too great for any aim among the aims or any purpose among the purposes to be accomplished except through His help, His enabling and His beneficence. This is what is meant by our saying "there is no power nor strength except by God, the Most High, the Mighty." Thus it is established that the Chapter of the Opening, from its beginning to its end, corresponds to that dhikr, and the verses of this chapter serve as an explanation and elaboration of the five levels mentioned in that dhikr.

**The third benefit:** He said ﴿You alone we worship﴾, placing "You" (*iyyāka*) before "we worship" (*naʿbudu*), and He did not say "we worship You" (*naʿbuduka*). In this there are several points:

**[p. 199]**

First: God, exalted is He, mentioned Himself first so that the worshipper would be alerted that the One worshipped is the true God, and so he would not grow lax in glorifying Him or turn right and left. It is related that one of the professional wrestlers, a master (ustadh), wrestled with a coarse peasant (rustaqi), and the peasant threw that master down several times. It was said to the peasant, "This is so-and-so, the master," and at once he was thrown down by him. This was only because of his reverence for him. Likewise here: He made Himself known first, so that worship would be accompanied by reverence and would not be mixed with heedlessness.

Second: if acts of obedience are burdensome to you, and acts of worship such as standing, bowing, and prostration are difficult for you, then first recall His saying *iyyaka na'budu* ("You alone we worship"), so that you remember Me and the knowledge of Me is present in your heart. When you remember My majesty, My greatness, and My might, and know that I am your Lord and you are My servant, I make those acts of worship easy for you. An example of this: whoever wants to lift a heavy body first takes something that increases his strength and power. So when the servant wants to bear the arduous and severe obligations, he first takes the electuary of the knowledge of divine lordship from the pharmacy (*bustuqa*) of His saying *iyyaka*, until he becomes able to bear the weight of servitude. Another example: the lover who is beaten for the sake of his beloved, in the presence of his beloved, finds that beating easy. Likewise here: when he beholds the beauty of *iyyaka*, the burden of servitude becomes easy for him to bear.

Third: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are conscious of God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember [God], and then they are seeing clearly﴾ [al-A'raf: 201]. So when the soul is touched by an impulse from Satan, through laziness, heedlessness, or idleness, they remember the presence of God's majesty from the dawning point of His saying *iyyaka na'budu*, and they become seeing, prepared to perform acts of worship and obedience.

Fourth: when you say *na'buduka* ("we worship You") and begin first by mentioning the worship of yourself without mentioning to whom that worship is directed, it is possible that Iblis would say, "This worship is for the idols, or for bodies, or for the sun or the moon." But when you reverse this order and say first *iyyaka* and then, second, *na'budu*, your first saying *iyyaka* is explicit that the one intended and worshipped is God, exalted is He. Thus this is more eloquent in affirming divine unity (tawhid) and further from any possibility of associationism (shirk).

Fifth: the Eternal, Necessary of Existence through Itself (al-qadim al-wajib li-dhatihi) precedes in existence the originated, Possible of Existence through Itself (al-muhdath al-mumkin li-dhatihi). Therefore His mention must precede all mentions. For this reason He placed *iyyaka* before *na'budu*, so that the mention of the Real would precede the mention of creation.

Sixth: some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: whoever, in a time of blessing, looks to the Benefactor and not to the blessing, will look, in a time of trial, to the One who tests and not to the trial. Then he will be immersed in every state in the knowledge of the Real, glorified is He, and whoever is like this will always be in the highest ranks of happiness. But whoever, in a time of blessing, looks to the blessing and not to the Benefactor, will look, in a time of trial, to the trial and not to the One who tests. Thus he will be immersed at all times in preoccupation with other than God, and he will always be in wretchedness. For in the time of possessing a blessing he is fearful of its loss, so he is in torment; and in the time of losing a blessing he is afflicted with disgrace and punishment, so he is in pure chains and shackles. For this very reason He said to the nation of Moses: *Remember My blessing*; and He said to the nation of Muhammad, peace be upon him: *Remember Me, and I will remember you*.

**[p. 200]**

Having understood this, we say: He placed *iyyaka* before *na'budu* only so that the servant would be fully absorbed in beholding the light of the majesty of *iyyaka*. When this is the case, at the time of performing worship he is established in the very essence of Paradise, as God, exalted is He, said in the hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me by voluntary acts until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing and his sight..."

Seventh: if it were said *na'buduka* ("we worship You") it would not indicate the negation of their worship of others, for there is no impossibility in their worshipping God and also worshipping other than God, as is the practice of the polytheists. But when He said *iyyaka na'budu*, it indicated that they worship Him and do not worship other than God.

Eighth: this *nun* is the *nun* of majesty (nun al-'azama), as if it were said to him: "When you are outside the prayer, do not say 'we,' even if you are among a thousand thousand servants. But when you have engaged in prayer and manifested servitude to Us, then say *na'budu*, so that it becomes evident to all that everyone who is a servant to Us is the king of this world and the Hereafter."

Ninth: if he said *iyyaka a'budu* ("I worship You"), that would be arrogance, meaning: "I am the worshipper." But when he said *iyyaka na'budu*, it means: "I am one of Your servants." The former is arrogance, the latter humility, and whoever is humble for God, God raises him, and whoever is arrogant, God brings him low.

If someone says: "All that you have mentioned is present in the saying *al-hamdu lillah* ('Praise belongs to God'), although there He placed the mention of praise before the mention of God." The answer is that the word *al-hamd* may be for God or for other than God. So when you say *lillah* ("to God"), praise is restricted to being for God. But if He had placed the word *na'budu* first, it would have been possible that it is for God and possible that it is for other than God, and that would be disbelief. The point is that since praise was permissible for other than God, in outward appearance, just as it is permissible for God, therefore placing praise first was good. Here, however, since worship is not permissible for other than God, He therefore placed *iyyaka* before *na'budu*, so the worship is definitely directed to God, and no possibility remains in the statement that worship could fall upon other than God.

**The Fourth Benefit:** One may say: the *nun* in *na'budu* is either the *nun* of plurality or the *nun* of majesty. The first is invalid, because a single person is not a plural. The second is also invalid, because at the performance of worship the fitting attitude for a human being is to describe himself with humility and lowliness, not with greatness and exaltation.

Know that this can be answered from several aspects, each of which indicates a profound wisdom.

**The first aspect:** the intended *nun* here is the *nun* of plurality, and this points out that it is better for a person to perform the prayer in congregation. The benefit of congregational prayer is known in its proper place, and it is indicated by his, peace be upon him, saying: "The first takbir in congregational prayer is better than the world and what is in it." Then we say: if a person has eaten garlic or onion, he is not permitted to attend the congregation, lest any person be harmed by it. So it is as if He, exalted is He, says: "This act of obedience, which has this great reward, its reward does not suffice to permit that one Muslim be harmed by the smell of garlic and onion. If this reward does not suffice for that, how could it suffice for harming a Muslim? And how could it suffice for slander, backbiting, and tale-bearing?"

**The second aspect:** when a man is praying in congregation, he says *na'budu*, and by it he intends that group. If he is praying alone, what is intended is: "I worship You, and the angels are with me in the worship." So by His saying *na'budu* is meant himself together with all the angels who worship God.

**The third aspect:** believers are brothers. If he said *iyyaka a'budu*, he would have mentioned the worship of himself without mentioning the worship of others. But when he said *iyyaka na'budu*, he mentioned his own worship and the worship of all believers, east and west. So it is as if he strove to set right the concerns of all other believers. When he does this, God settles his concerns, in accordance with His, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever fulfills a need for a Muslim, God fulfills for him all his needs."

**[p. 201]**

**The fourth aspect:** it is as if He, exalted is He, said to the servant: "When you praised Us by saying *al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin, al-Rahman al-Rahim, Maliki yawm al-din*, and you committed to Us all the praises of this world and the Hereafter, your station has become great before Us, and your position has been firmly established in Our presence. So do not limit yourself to setting right your concerns alone, but set right the needs of all Muslims. So say: *iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in*."

**The fifth aspect:** it is as if the servant says: "My God, my worship has not reached the point where I deserve to mention it alone, for it is mixed with aspects of deficiency. But I mix it with the worship of all worshippers, and I mention all of it in one expression, and I say: *iyyaka na'budu*."

Here is a legal issue: if a man sells ten slaves to another, the buyer either accepts them all or does not accept any of them, and he does not have the right to accept some and reject others in that same transaction. Likewise here: when the servant says *iyyaka na'budu*, he has offered to the presence of God all the worship of worshippers. It does not befit His generosity to distinguish some from others and accept some while rejecting others. Either He would reject all, which is not permissible, because His saying *iyyaka na'budu* includes the worship of the angels, the prophets, and the saints; or He accepts all, and in that case this speaker's worship becomes accepted through the blessing of the acceptance of the worship of others. The meaning is as if the servant says: "My God, if my worship is not accepted, then do not reject me, for I am not alone in this worship; rather we are many. If I do not deserve answer and acceptance, then I intercede with You through the worship of all other worshippers. So answer me."

**The Fifth Benefit:** know that whoever knows the benefits of worship finds pleasure in engaging in it, and engaging in other things becomes burdensome for him. Its explanation is from several aspects:

**The first:** perfection is loved for its own sake, and the most perfect and strongest states of a human being, in terms of being happiness, are his occupation with the worship of God. For his heart is illuminated by the light of divinity, his tongue is honored by the honor of remembrance and recitation, and his limbs are beautified by the beauty of serving God. These states are the most noble of human ranks and the highest of human degrees. So when attaining these states is the greatest of human happinesses in the present, and it also necessarily leads to the most perfect happiness in the future, whoever has comprehended these states, the burden of acts of obedience is removed from him, and their sweetness becomes great in his heart.

**The second:** worship is a trust (amanah), as is shown by God's saying: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust to the heavens﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72], and the fulfillment of a trust is obligatory by reason and by law, as shown by His saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. The fulfillment of a trust is an attribute of perfection that is loved for its own sake. Moreover, fulfilling a trust on one side is a cause for fulfilling a trust on the other side. One of the Companions said: "I saw a bedouin arrive at the door of the mosque. He dismounted from his she-camel and left her, entered the mosque, and prayed with tranquility and dignity, and supplicated for whatever he wished. We were amazed. When he came out, he did not find his she-camel, so he said: 'My God, I have fulfilled Your trust, so where is my trust?' The narrator said: 'Our amazement increased. Then, before long, a man came on his she-camel, his hand having been cut off, and handed the she-camel over to him.'" The point is that when he preserved God's trust, God preserved his trust. This is what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying to Ibn 'Abbas: "O boy, guard God, and He will guard you. Guard God in your solitude, and He will guard you in your wanderings."

**The third:** engaging in worship is a transition from the world of delusion to the world of joy, and from preoccupation with created beings to the presence of the Real. This necessarily produces the perfection of pleasure and delight. It is related about Abu Hanifa that a snake fell from the ceiling, and the people scattered, while Abu Hanifa was in prayer and did not notice it. And gangrene infected one of the limbs of 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, and they needed to amputate that limb. When he began the prayer, they cut off that limb from him, and 'Urwa did not perceive that cutting. And from the Messenger of

**[p. 202]**

[Continuation of the narration:] ...of Allah (ﷺ) that when he began the prayer, they would hear from his chest a buzzing like the buzzing of a boiling cauldron. Whoever finds this far-fetched should recite His words, exalted is He: ﴿When they saw him, they were struck with awe of him and cut their hands﴾ [Yusuf: 31]. The women's hearts were overcome by the beauty of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and that overcoming reached the point that they cut their hands without feeling it. If this is possible with regard to a human being, then it is all the more possible when the majesty of Allah overwhelms the heart. Moreover, one who enters upon a awe-inspiring king may pass by his parents and children while he looks at them and does not recognize them, because the dominance of that awe prevents the heart from being aware of them. If this is possible regarding a created, accountable king, then it is all the more possible regarding the Creator of the worlds.

Then the scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq) said: worship ('ibadah, devotional service) has three levels.

The first level: to worship Allah out of hope for reward or fear of punishment. This is what is called worship, and this level is very low and base, because what he actually worships is that reward. He has made the Truth a means to attaining the desired goal. Whoever makes a thing of the states of creation the ultimate goal and makes the Truth a means to it is extremely despicable.

The second level: to worship Allah in order to honour himself by worshipping Him, or to honour himself by accepting His obligations, or to honour himself by being affiliated with Him. This level is higher than the first, but it is also not complete, because the ultimate object is other than Allah.

The third level: to worship Allah because He is God and Creator, and because he is His servant. Divinity entails awe and might, and servanthood ('ubudiyyah, state of being a servant) entails humility and abasement. This is the highest station and the most noble rank. This is what is called servanthood, and the words of the worshipper at the beginning of the prayer point to it: "I pray to Allah." For if he were to say "I pray for Allah's reward, or to flee from His punishment," his prayer would be invalid.

Know that worship and servanthood are a lofty and noble station, and verses indicate this:

The first: His words, exalted is He, at the end of Surat al-Hijr: ﴿We know that your breast is constricted by what they say. So glorify your Lord with praise and be among the prostrators. And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 97–99]. The argument from these is in two respects.

One: He said, "and worship your Lord until certainty comes to you," commanding Muhammad (peace be upon him) to be constant in worship until death comes to him. Its meaning is that it is not permissible to neglect worship at any time, and this indicates the supreme exaltedness of the matter of worship.

The second: He said, "We know that your breast is constricted by what they say." Then He commanded him with four things: glorification, which is His words "so glorify"; praise, which is His words "with praise of your Lord"; prostration, which is His words "and be among the prostrators"; and worship, which is His words "and worship your Lord until certainty comes to you." This indicates that worship removes constriction of the heart and produces expansion of the breast, and that is only because worship necessitates the return from creation to the Truth, and that necessitates the removal of constriction of the heart.

The second verse on the nobility of servanthood: His words, exalted is He: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra: 1]. Had servanthood not been the noblest station, He would not have described him with this attribute at the highest stations of the Ascension (mi'raj). Some have said: servanthood is nobler than prophethood (risalah, messengership), because through servanthood one turns from creation to the Truth, while through prophethood one turns from the Truth to creation. Also, through servanthood one withdraws from worldly dispositions, while through prophethood one engages with them. What is fitting for the servant is to withdraw from dispositions. Also, the servant has his Master take charge of his affairs, while the messenger is the one who takes charge of the affairs of the community. How far apart the two are!

[Page 203]

The third verse on the nobility of servanthood: when Jesus first spoke, he said: ﴿I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam: 30]. His mention of this word became a cause of his mother's purity and of the innocence of his existence from slander, and it became a key to all good and a repeller of all calamities. Also, since the first words of Jesus were the mention of servanthood, its outcome was elevation, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿and raising you to Me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55]. The point is that whoever claimed servanthood by word was raised to Paradise, so how could one who claims it by deed for seventy years remain deprived of Paradise?

The fourth verse: His words, exalted is He, to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14]. He commanded him, after tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), to worship Him, because tawhid is the root and servanthood is the branch; tawhid is the tree and servanthood is the fruit, and neither subsists without the other. These verses thus indicate the nobility of servanthood.

As for rational argument, it is evident: the servant is originated, possible in existence in himself. Were it not for the effect of the power of the Truth upon him, he would remain in the darkness of nonexistence and in the annihilation of annihilation, and existence would not be attained for him, let alone the perfections of existence. When the power of the Truth attached itself to him and the effects of His generosity and bringing-into-being overflowed upon him, existence and the perfections of existence were attained for him. There is no meaning to his being the object of the power of the Truth and the object of the Truth's bringing-into-being except servanthood. So every nobility, perfection, delight, excellence, joy, distinction, and virtue that the servant attains is attained only through servanthood. Thus it is established that servanthood is the key to goods, the title of felicities, the dawning-point of levels, and the spring of honours. For this reason the servant says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾. Ali (may Allah honour his face) used to say: "It is enough honour for me that I am Your servant, and enough nobility for me that You are my Lord. O Allah, I have found You as God as You willed, so make me a servant as You willed."

Point six: know that stations are confined to two: knowledge of lordship (rububiyyah, the state of being Lord) and knowledge of servanthood. When the two come together, the covenant mentioned in His words is fulfilled: ﴿Fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. As for knowledge of lordship, its perfection is mentioned in His words: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ ﴿Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾. The servant's transition from prior nonexistence to existence indicates that He is God; the attainment of goods and felicities by the servant during his existence indicates that He is Lord, Most Gracious, Most Merciful; and the states of the servant's return indicate that He is Sovereign of the Day of Recompense. When one comprehends these attributes, knowledge of lordship is attained to its utmost limits. After that comes knowledge of servanthood, which has a beginning, a perfection, a first and a last. Its beginning and first stage is engagement in servanthood, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿You alone we worship﴾. Its perfection is that the servant knows that there is no power to turn away from disobedience to Allah except by Allah's protection, and no strength to obey Allah except by Allah's enabling. At that point he seeks help from Allah in attaining all his aims, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾. When fulfilment of the covenant of lordship and the covenant of servanthood is complete, what follows is the request for benefit and fruit, which is His words: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. This is a noble, lofty, exalted order, and it is impossible for the intellects to conceive of any other order more noble than it.

Point seven: One may say: His whole statement, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, Sovereign of the Day of Recompense," is in the third person, and His words "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" shift from the third person to the second person. What is the benefit in this? We say: there are several aspects to this:

The first: the worshipper was a stranger at the beginning of the prayer, so he praised Allah with third-person expressions up to His words "Sovereign of the Day of Recompense." Then, as it were, Allah says to him: "You have praised Me and acknowledged that I am God, Lord, Most Gracious, Most Merciful, Sovereign of the Day of Recompense. How excellent a servant you are! We have raised the veil and replaced distance with nearness, so speak in direct address and say: 'You alone we worship.'"

[Page 204]

The second aspect: the best of requests is that which is made by direct address. Do you not see that when the prophets, peace be upon them, asked their Lord, they addressed Him directly, saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]; ﴿Our Lord, forgive us﴾ [al-Hashr: 10]; ﴿My Lord, grant me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 83]; ﴿My Lord, show me﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. The reason is that a response from the Generous One by way of direct address and speech is far removed; and also, worship is service, and service is better in the presence (of the one served).

The third aspect: from the beginning of the surah up to His words "You alone we worship" is praise, and praise is better in the third person; and from His words "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help" to the end of the surah is supplication, and supplication is better in the presence (of the one addressed).

The fourth aspect: when the worshipper began the prayer and said, "I intend to pray seeking nearness to Allah," he intends the attainment of nearness. Then after this intention he mentioned kinds of praise of Allah, so Allah's generosity required that He answer him in attaining that nearness, and so He moved him from the station of the third person to the station of the second person, and said: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾.
