Section Six
On His words: ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾

Know that it has been established by rational proofs that there is no turning away from disobedience to Allah except by Allah's protection, and no power to obey Allah except by Allah's enabling. Several proofs from reason and transmitted texts indicate this. As for reason, the proofs are of several kinds:

The first: the capable agent is able to act or refrain equally. As long as the determining factor (al-murajjih) has not come about, the preponderance does not come about. That determining factor is not from the servant, for otherwise it would regress in seeking; so it is from Allah, exalted is He. Thus it is established that the servant cannot undertake an action except by Allah's help.

The second: all created beings seek the true religion and the correct belief, while being equal in capacity, intellect, earnestness, and seeking. So the success of some in reaching the truth can only be through the help of a helper, and that helper is none other than Allah, exalted is He; for if that helper were a human being or an angel, the seeking would revert to him.

The third: a person may be asked to do something for a long period and not do it; then, in the course of some state or time, he does it and undertakes it. That state does not occur for him unless a firm motive arises in his heart that calls him to that action. The casting of that motive into the heart and the removal of the opposing motives are nothing but from Allah, exalted is He, and there is no meaning to help except that.

As for transmitted texts, verses indicate this. The first of them: His words, ﴿and You alone we ask for help﴾. The second: His words, ﴿Seek help through Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 128]. The Jabriyya (determinists) and the Qadariyya (voluntarists) have disputed over this verse. As for the Jabriyya, they said: if the servant were independent in the action, there would be no benefit in seeking help for the action. As for the Qadariyya, they said: seeking help is only fitting if the servant is able to perform the act itself, so help from another is void; but if he is not able to act, seeking help has no benefit.

In my view, power does not affect the action except together with a firm motive, so the help sought is an expression for creating a firm motive and removing the diverting motive. Let us mention some of the subtleties and benefits in this statement:

Point one: one may say: seeking help for an action is only fitting before beginning the action, and here He mentioned His words, ﴿You alone we worship﴾, and then right after it, ﴿and You alone we ask for help.﴾ What is the wisdom in this? The answer has several aspects:

The first: as if the worshipper says, "I have begun the worship, so I seek Your help in completing it. Do not prevent me from completing it by death, or by illness, or by the turning of hearts and their changing."

Second: It is as if the human being says: "O my God, I have come to You with myself, but I have a heart that flees from me, so I seek Your help in bringing it present." And how (could it not be so), when the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful"? This indicates that a person cannot bring the heart present except with Allah's help.

Third: I do not want any helper besides You, neither Jibril nor Mika'il; rather I want You alone, and in this path I follow the Khalil (the Intimate Friend, i.e., Ibrahim), peace be upon him. For when Nimrod bound his feet and hands and threw him into the fire, Jibril, peace be upon him, came and said to him: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you, no." He said: "Ask Him." He said: "My knowledge of my state is enough of a request for me." Indeed, perhaps I may exceed the Khalil in this regard, because his feet and hands were bound and nothing more; but as for me, my feet are bound so I do not walk, my hands so I do not move them, my eyes so I do not look with them, my ears so I do not hear with them, and my tongue so I do not speak with it. The Khalil was overlooking the fire of Nimrod, and I am overlooking the fire of Hell. So just as the Khalil, peace be upon him, did not accept any helper other than You, likewise I do not want any helper other than You. "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help." It is as if He, exalted, says: "You have done the deed of the Khalil and gone beyond it, so We also increase the reward, for We said there: ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾ [al-Anbiya: 69]. As for you, We have saved you from the fire, brought you to Paradise, and increased for you the hearing of the Eternal Speech and the vision of the Eternal Existent. Just as We said to the fire of Nimrod, ‘﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim﴾,’ so likewise the fire of Hell says to you: ‘Pass over, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flame.’"

Fourth: "You alone we ask for help" means: I seek help from no one other than You. That is because that other cannot help me unless You enable him to give that help; so if the help of another is not complete except by Your help, then let us cut off this intermediary and confine ourselves to Your help.

Fifth: His saying "You alone we worship" necessitates the attainment of a great rank for the soul through the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and this begets self-admiration. Therefore He followed it with His saying "and You alone we ask for help," to indicate that this rank obtained through worship was not achieved by the strength of the servant, but was achieved only by the help of Allah. Thus the purpose of mentioning "and You alone we ask for help" is the removal of self-admiration and the annihilation of that pride and arrogance.

[Page 206]

**Section Seven**

On His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, and in it are several benefits.

**The first benefit:** Someone may say: The one who prays must be a believer, and every believer is already guided. So the one praying is guided. When he says "Guide us," it amounts to saying that whoever has already received guidance still seeks guidance. This would be a request for something already obtained, which is impossible. The scholars answered this objection in several ways.

**The first answer:** What is meant is the path of the earlier ones in bearing great hardships for the sake of Allah's pleasure. It is related that Nuh (peace be upon him) would be struck several times each day until he fainted, and each time he would say: "O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know." If it is objected that our Prophet (ﷺ) said this only once, while he himself would say it many times each day, then it follows that Nuh (peace be upon him) was superior to him. The answer is this: since what is meant by His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is to ask Allah Most High for those noble character traits, and the Messenger (ﷺ) would recite al-Fatiha several times each day, the Messenger's (ﷺ) uttering this phrase was more frequent than Nuh's (peace be upon him) uttering it.

**The second answer:** The scholars have explained that every character trait has two extremes, deficiency and excess, both of which are blameworthy, while the truth lies in the middle. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143]. That middle is justice and correctness. The believer, after knowing Allah through proof, has become a believer who is guided. But after attaining this state, he must still know the justice that is the balanced line between the extremes of excess and deficiency in appetitive actions, in angry actions, and in the manner of spending wealth. So the believer asks Allah Most High to guide him to the straight path, which is the middle between the extremes of excess and deficiency in all character traits and all deeds. According to this explanation, the objection disappears.

**The third answer:** When the believer knows Allah through a single proof, there is no existing thing among the categories of possible beings that does not contain proofs of Allah's existence, knowledge, power, generosity, mercy, and wisdom. Indeed, a person's religion may be sound on the basis of a single proof while he remains heedless of all the other proofs. So His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ means: "Make us know, O our God, the manner in which everything points to Your essence and Your attributes, Your power, and Your knowledge." According to this interpretation, the objection disappears.

**The fourth answer:** Allah Most High said: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura 42:52–53]. He also said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am 6:153]. That straight path is for a person to turn away from everything other than Allah and to face Allah with the entirety of his heart, thought, and remembrance. So His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ means that Allah should guide him to the straight path described by the attribute just mentioned. For example, he should become such that if he were commanded to slaughter his son, he would obey, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) did; if he were commanded to submit so that another would slaughter him, he would obey, as Isma'il (peace be upon him) did; if he were commanded to throw himself into the sea, he would obey, as Yunus (peace be upon him) did; if he were commanded, after reaching the highest level of rank, to become a student of one who is more knowledgeable than him, he would obey, as Musa did with al-Khidr (peace be upon them both); and if he were commanded to endure, in enjoining good and forbidding evil, being killed and cut in half, he would obey, as Yahya and Zakariyya (peace be upon them both) did. Therefore, what is meant by His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ is to follow the prophets of Allah in patience under hardships and steadfastness when trials descend. There is no doubt that this is a severe and terrifying station, since most of creation has no strength for it. Yet we say: O people, do not fear and do not grieve, for no matter in the religion of Allah becomes narrow without becoming wide. In this verse there is something that indicates ease and facility, for He Most High did not say "the path of those who struck and killed," but rather said: ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾. So let your intention, when reciting this verse, be to say: "O my God, I saw that my father committed major sins as I did, and advanced into disobedience as I did. Then I saw that when his death approached, he repented and turned back to You, so You judged for him salvation from the Fire and success in Paradise. He is among those upon whom You bestowed favor, by granting him the ability to repent, and then by accepting his repentance. So I say: Guide us to a path like that straight path, seeking the rank of those who repent. And when You grant it, seek to follow the stations of the prophets (peace be upon them)." This is the explanation of His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾.

**The fifth answer:** It is as if a person says on the road: The multitude of loved ones pulls me toward one path, enemies toward a second path, and Satan toward a third. The same applies to appetite, anger, hatred, and envy. Likewise, the same applies to denial of attributes (ta'til), anthropomorphism (tashbih), determinism (jabr), free will (qadar), postponement (irja'), threat (wa'id), rejection (rafd), and rebellion (khuruj). The intellect is weak, life is short, the craft is long, experience is perilous, and judgment is difficult. I have been bewildered by all of this, so guide me to a path by which I may exit toward Paradise. The "straight" (mustaqim) is the upright one with no harshness in it.

It is related of Ibrahim ibn Adham that he was traveling to the House of Allah when he came upon a Bedouin on his camel. The Bedouin said: "O shaykh, where are you going?" Ibrahim said: "To the House of Allah." The Bedouin said: "It seems you are mad. I see you have no mount and no provisions, and the journey is long." Ibrahim said: "I have many mounts, but you do not see them." He said: "And what are they?" Ibrahim said: "When a calamity descends upon me, I ride the mount of patience. When a blessing descends upon me, I ride the mount of gratitude. When decree descends upon me, I ride the mount of contentment. And when the self calls me to something, I know that what remains of my life is less than what has passed." The Bedouin said: "Proceed, by Allah's permission, for you are the rider and I am the one on foot."

**The sixth answer:** Some said: the straight path is Islam. Others said: it is the Qur'an. But this is not correct, because His saying ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ is an apposition (badal) to "the straight path." If that is so, the meaning is: "Guide us to the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor among those who came before us." But the nations that preceded us did not have the Qur'an or Islam. If this is invalid, then it is established that what is meant is: "Guide us to the path of those who are truthful and deserving of Paradise." He said "the path" (al-sirat) and did not say "the way" (al-sabil) or "the road" (al-tariq), even though all of these are one in meaning, so that the word "sirat" would remind one of the path of Hell (sirat Jahannam), and thus the person would be in greater fear and awe.

**The second explanation of "Guide us" (ihdina):** That is, keep us steadfast upon the guidance You have bestowed upon us. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:8], meaning: keep us firm upon guidance. For how many scholars have had a weak doubt occur to their minds, and so they deviated, were humbled, and turned away from the upright religion and the straight method.

**The second benefit:** Someone may say: Why did he say "guide us" and not "guide me"? The answer is in two parts.

**The first:** The more general a supplication is, the closer it is to being answered. Some scholars used to say to their students: When you read in the preface (khutba) of a book by an earlier scholar, "May Allah be pleased with you and with the community of the Muslims," if you intend yourself in your words "May Allah be pleased with you," that is good, and otherwise there is no fault. But beware of forgetting me in your words "and with the community of the Muslims." For his saying "May Allah be pleased with you" is a specific supplication, which may not be accepted. As for his saying "and with the community of the Muslims," there must be among the Muslims someone who deserves to be answered. And if Allah answers the supplication for some, He is too generous to reject it for the rest. For this reason, the Sunnah (the Prophet's established practice) is that when one wishes to mention a supplication, he first sends blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then supplicates, and then concludes the speech by sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) again. For Allah Most High answers the one who supplicates in his prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ). Then, if the supplication is answered at both of its ends, it is impossible for it to be rejected in its middle.

**The second:** The Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "Invoke Allah with tongues with which you have not disobeyed Him." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and who among us has such tongues?" He said: "One of you should supplicate for another, for you have not disobeyed with his tongue, and he has not disobeyed with yours."

**The third:** It is as if he is saying: "O servant, did you not say at the beginning of the surah, 'All praise is for Allah,' and you did not say 'I praise Allah'? So you first mentioned the praise of all who praise. Likewise, at the time of supplication, include them, and say 'guide us.'"

**The fourth:** It is as if the servant says: "I heard Your Messenger say: 'The community is mercy, and division is punishment.' So when I wished to praise You, I mentioned the praise of all, and I said 'All praise is for Allah.' When I mentioned worship, I mentioned the worship of all, and I said 'You alone we worship.' When I mentioned seeking help, I mentioned the seeking of help of all, and I said 'You alone we ask for help.' Thus, when I sought guidance, I sought it for all, and I said 'Guide us to the straight path.' When I sought to follow the righteous, I sought to follow all of them, and I said 'the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor.' And when I sought to flee from those who are rejected, I fled from all of them, and I said 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray.' So since I did not part from the prophets and the righteous in this world, I hope not to part from them on the Day of Resurrection." Allah Most High said: ﴿Those will be with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor of the prophets...﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:69], and so on.

**The third benefit:** Know that the people of geometry (handasa) said: "The straight line is the shortest line connecting two points." The result is that the straight line is shorter than all crooked lines. So it is as if the servant is saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ for several reasons:

**The first:** It is the closest and shortest of lines, and I am weak, so only the straight path suits my weakness.

**The second:** The straight is one, while everything else is crooked, and some of the crooked paths resemble each other in their crookedness, so the way would be confused for me. But the straight path is not resembled by anything else. So it is farther from fear and calamities and closer to safety.

**The third:** The straight path leads to the intended goal, while the crooked one does not lead to it.

**The fourth:** The straight does not change, while the crooked changes. For these reasons, he asked for the straight path. And Allah knows best.

**Chapter Eight**

**On the exegesis of His words: ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾. It contains several benefits.**

**The first benefit: on the definition of blessing (niʿmah).** Scholars differ on it. Some said it is an expression for a benefit conferred as a kindness to another. Others said it is a good benefit conferred as a kindness to another. They said: "We added this qualifier because blessing deserves gratitude, and if it is ugly, it does not deserve gratitude." The truth is that this qualifier is not valid, because it is possible for gratitude to be deserved for a kindness even if the act is forbidden. The basis for deserving gratitude is different from the basis for sin and punishment, so what prevents them from being combined? Do you not see that a sinner deserves gratitude for his favour and blame for his disobedience to Allah? Why should it not be the same here?

Let us return to explaining the stated definition. As for our saying "a benefit," it is because pure harm is not a blessing. As for our saying "conferred as a kindness," it is because if it were a true benefit but the doer intended by it his own benefit and not the benefit of the recipient, it would not be a blessing. This is like one who is kind to his slave-girl in order to profit from her.

Once you know the definition of blessing, branches follow from it:

**First branch:** Know that every benefit that reaches creation, and every removal of harm, is from Allah Most High, as He said: ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [al-Naḥl: 53]. Blessing is of three kinds:

First: a blessing that Allah alone brings into being, such as creating and providing.

Second: a blessing that apparently comes from someone other than Allah, but in reality it also comes from Allah Most High. This is because He is the Creator of that blessing, the Creator of that benefactor, and the Creator of the motive to bestow that blessing in the heart of that benefactor. However, when Allah Most High causes that blessing to pass through the hand of that servant, that servant is thanked. Yet the one truly thanked is Allah Most High. For this reason He said: ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final return﴾ [Luqmān: 14]. He began with Himself, to alert that the favour of creatures is not complete except through the favour of Allah.

Third: blessings that reach us from Allah because of our obedience. These too are from Allah Most High, because if Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, had not granted us success in acts of obedience, helped us to them, guided us to them, and removed obstacles from us, we would not have reached any of them. Thus it becomes clear from this explanation that all blessings are in reality from Allah Most High.

**Second branch:** The first of Allah's blessings upon His servants is that He created them alive. Both reason and transmitted text indicate this. As for reason: a thing is not a blessing unless it can be benefited from, and benefit is not possible except when life exists, for an inanimate or dead thing cannot benefit from anything. Thus it is established that the root of all blessings is life. As for transmitted text: He Most High said: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. Then He said immediately after it: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. He began with mentioning life and then mentioned the things from which one benefits. This indicates that the root of all blessings is life.

**Third branch:** Scholars differ on whether Allah has a blessing upon the disbeliever or not. Some of our companions said: Allah has no blessing upon the disbeliever. The Muʿtazilah (a rationalist theological school) said: Allah has upon the disbeliever a religious blessing and a worldly blessing.

Our companions argued for the soundness of their view with the Qur'an and with reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses. The first is His saying: ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾. This is because if Allah had a blessing upon the disbeliever, they would be included under His saying: ﴿You have blessed﴾. In that case, His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed﴾ would be a request for the path of the disbelievers, and that is false. Thus this verse establishes that Allah has no blessing upon the disbelievers.

If they say: "His saying 'the path' removes this," we reply: His saying ﴿the path of those You have blessed﴾ is in apposition (badal) to His saying ﴿the straight path﴾. So the meaning would be: Guide us to the path of those You have blessed. In that case the objection mentioned returns.

The second verse is His saying: ﴿Let not those who disbelieve think that Our respite for them is good for themselves. We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 178].

As for reason: the blessings of this world, compared with the punishment of the Hereafter which is everlasting, are few, like a drop in the sea. Such a thing is not a blessing. The evidence is that one who puts poison in a sweet dish does not make the benefit obtained from it a blessing, because that benefit is trivial compared with the great harm. So it is the same here.

As for those who said that Allah has many blessings upon the disbeliever, they argued with verses:

The first is His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, so that you may be mindful of Him. He who made the earth a bed for you and the sky a canopy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21–22]. Thus He alerted that obedience to Allah is obligatory upon all because of these great blessings.

The second is His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. He mentioned this in the context of bestowing favour and explaining blessings.

The third is His saying Most High: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40].

The fourth is His saying Most High: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13], and the saying of Iblīs: ﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 17]. If blessings did not exist, gratitude would not be required, and their failure to be grateful would not entail any problem, because gratitude is not possible except when a blessing exists.

**The second benefit:** His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed﴾ indicates the imamate (leadership) of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. This is because we mentioned that the meaning of the verse is: Guide us to the path of those You have blessed. Allah Most High has clarified in another verse who those upon whom He has bestowed blessing are, saying: ﴿So those are with those whom Allah has blessed, of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisā': 69]. There is no doubt that the head and leader of the truthful (ṣiddīqīn) is Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him. So the meaning of the verse is that Allah commanded us to seek the guidance upon which Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq and all the truthful stood. If Abū Bakr had been an oppressor, it would not have been permissible to follow him. Thus, by what we have mentioned, the indication of this verse for the imamate of Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, is established.

**The third benefit:** His saying ﴿those You have blessed﴾ encompasses everyone upon whom Allah has bestowed a blessing. This blessing is either the blessing of this world or the blessing of religion. Since the first is invalid, it is established that the intended meaning is the blessing of religion. We say: every religious blessing other than faith is conditional upon the attainment of faith. As for the blessing which is faith itself, it is possible for it to be attained without the other religious blessings. This indicates that what is intended by His saying ﴿You have blessed﴾ is the blessing of faith. So the sum of the meaning of His saying ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those You have blessed﴾ is that it is a request for the blessing of faith.

Once this principle is established, rulings follow from it:

**First ruling:** Since it is established that the intended meaning of this blessing is the blessing of faith, and the wording of the verse is explicit that Allah Most High is the One who bestows this blessing, it is established that the Creator of faith and the Giver of faith is Allah Most High. This indicates the falsity of the Muʿtazilah's view. Moreover, since faith is the greatest of blessings, if the servant were its doer, the servant's bestowal would be nobler and higher than Allah's bestowal. If that were so, it would not be fitting for Allah to mention His bestowal in the context of exalting it.

**Second ruling:** The believer must not remain eternally in the Fire. This is because His saying ﴿You have blessed﴾ is mentioned in the context of exalting this bestowal. If it had no effect in averting everlasting punishment, it would be of little benefit, and it would not be fitting for Allah Most High to mention it in the context of exalting it.

**Third ruling:** The verse indicates that it is not obligatory upon Allah to provide what is good and best in religion. This is because if guidance were obligatory upon Allah, it would not be a bestowal, since the performance of an obligation is not a bestowal. And since Allah Most High called it a bestowal, we know that it is not obligatory.

**Fourth ruling:** The bestowal cannot mean that Allah Most High empowered the responsible person to it, guided him to it, and removed his excuses and impediments from him. This is because all of that is present in the case of the disbelievers. Since Allah Most High specified some of the responsible persons with this bestowal, although this empowerment and removal of impediments is general to all, we know that the intended meaning of bestowal is not merely empowering him to it and removing obstacles from him.

**Chapter Nine**

**On His words Most High: ﴿not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾. It contains several benefits.**

**The first benefit:** It is well known that "those who have incurred anger" are the Jews, because of His saying Most High: ﴿Those whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He has become angry﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 60]. And "those who are astray" are the Christians, because of His saying Most High: ﴿They have already gone astray and led many astray and strayed from the right way﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 77]. It has been said that this view is weak, because deniers of the Creator and polytheists are more corrupt in religion than the Jews and Christians, so avoiding their religion would be more appropriate. Rather, it is better to interpret "those who have incurred anger" as referring to everyone who errs in outward actions, namely the sinners, and to interpret "those who are astray" as referring to everyone who errs in belief, because the wording is general and restriction contradicts the basic principle. It is also possible to say that "those who have incurred anger" are the disbelievers and "those who are astray" are the hypocrites. This is because He Most High began by mentioning the believers and praising them in five verses at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Then He followed with mention of the disbelievers, His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. Then He followed with mention of the hypocrites, His saying: ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. Similarly here, He began with mention of the believers, His saying ﴿You have blessed﴾, then followed with mention of the disbelievers, His saying ﴿not of those who have incurred anger﴾, then followed with mention of the hypocrites, His saying ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾.

**The second benefit:** Since Allah has ruled concerning them that they are astray, it is impossible for them to be believers. Otherwise, the true report of Allah would become false, and that is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is itself impossible.

**The third benefit:** His saying ﴿not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ indicates that none of the angels and prophets, upon them be peace, ever undertook an action contrary to the statement of those upon whom Allah has bestowed blessing, nor contrary to the belief of those upon whom Allah has bestowed blessing. This is because if such a thing had come from them, they would have strayed from the truth, according to His saying Most High: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yūnus: 32]. If they were astray, it would not be permissible to follow them or follow their way, and they would be outside His saying ﴿You have blessed﴾. Since that is false, we know from this verse the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the prophets and angels, upon them be peace.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 1, verse 7 (part 2 of 2):

The Fourth Benefit: Anger (ghadab) is a change that occurs when the blood of the heart boils out of the desire for revenge. Know that this is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. But here there is a universal rule: all the psychological attributes, I mean mercy, joy, happiness, anger, modesty, jealousy, deceit, trickery, arrogance and mockery, have beginnings and have ends. An example is anger: its beginning is the boiling of the blood of the heart, and its end is the desire to inflict harm upon the one who is angered against. Therefore the word "anger" as applied to Allah, the Exalted, is not to be understood in its beginning, which is the boiling of the blood of the heart, but rather in its end, which is the desire to harm. Likewise, modesty (haya') has a beginning, which is a sense of contraction that arises in the soul, and it has an aim, which is abstaining from the act. So the word "modesty" as applied to Allah is understood as abstaining from the act, not as contraction of the soul. This is a noble rule in this matter.

The Fifth Benefit: The Mu'tazilah said: Allah's anger against them indicates that they are the doers of ugly deeds by their own choice, for otherwise the anger against them would be an injustice from Allah, the Exalted. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: When the anger of Allah against them was mentioned and it was followed by mention of their being astray (dallin), this indicates that Allah's anger against them is the cause of their being astray. In that case, the attribute of Allah affects the attribute of the servant. But if we say that their being astray necessitates Allah's anger against them, then it would follow that the attribute of the servant affects the attribute of Allah, the Exalted, and that is impossible.

The Sixth Benefit: The beginning of the surah includes praise of Allah, extolling Him and commending Him, and its end includes censure of those who turn away from believing in Him and acknowledging obedience to Him. This indicates that the source of goods and the title of happiness is turning towards Allah, the Exalted, and the source of calamities and the head of fears is turning away from Allah, the Exalted, and distancing oneself from His obedience and abstaining from serving Him.

The Seventh Benefit: This verse indicates that those who are obligated (mukallafun) are three groups: the people of obedience, to whom the reference is in His saying "You have blessed (an'amta) them"; the people of disobedience, to whom the reference is in His saying "not of those who have earned anger (al-maghdub 'alayhim)"; and the people of ignorance regarding the religion of Allah and of disbelief, to whom the reference is in His saying "nor of those who are astray (al-dallin)."

If it is said: Why did He mention the disobedient before the disbelievers? We say: Because each person guards against disbelief, but may not guard against wickedness (fisq), so the latter was more important, and for this reason it was mentioned first.

The Eighth Benefit: In the verse there is a question, namely: Allah's anger arises only from His knowledge of the occurrence of the ugly deed and the offense from them. This knowledge either is said to be eternal (qadim) or originated (muhdath). If this knowledge is eternal, then why did He create it, and why did He bring it from non-existence into existence, while knowing that from its entry into existence they will gain nothing but everlasting punishment? Moreover, how is it conceivable that one who is angry at a thing would proceed to bring it into being and to create it? And if that knowledge is originated, then the Creator, the Exalted, would become a locus of originated events, and moreover it would necessitate that the bringing about of that knowledge depends on a prior knowledge, leading to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Its answer: Allah does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

The Ninth Benefit: In the verse there is another question, namely: whoever Allah has blessed cannot be one upon whom anger falls and cannot be among the astray. When He mentioned His saying "You have blessed them," what is the benefit in His mentioning after it "not of those who have earned anger and nor of the astray"? The answer: Faith is only perfected by hope and fear, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If the fear and hope of the believer were weighed, they would be balanced." So His saying "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed blessings" necessitates complete hope, and His saying "not of those who have earned anger, nor of the astray" necessitates complete fear. Then faith is strengthened with its two pillars and its two sides and reaches the limit of perfection.

The Tenth Benefit: In the verse there is another question: What is the wisdom in His making those accepted one group, namely those upon whom Allah has bestowed blessings, and those rejected two groups: those who have earned anger and the astray? The answer: Those upon whom Allah's blessings are complete are those who combined knowledge of the truth for its own sake and good for the sake of acting upon it. These are the ones meant by His saying "You have blessed them." If the condition of action is lacking, then they are the transgressors (fasaqah), and they are "those who have earned anger," as Allah, the Exalted, said: "And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein forever, and Allah has become angry with him and has cursed him" [An-Nisa: 93]. If the condition of knowledge is lacking, then they are "the astray," due to His saying, the Exalted: "So what is there after the truth but error?" [Yunus: 32]. This is the end of our discussion in the detailed explanation of each of the verses of this surah, and Allah knows best.
